Such clean energy solutions have some constraints. First, the initial investment costs and the costs of 
deploying such service is relatively expensive. Second, those sources rely on weather because the solar 
operates during sunny days. Additionally, their locations are also playing a great role in reducing the impact 
of such solutions [21]. This has eased the ways through which data centers can cut down on fossil fuel 
usage and lower their emissions of carbon. Major tech giants, have begun to integrate renewable energy 
sources into their data center operations [22]. 
• Apple's Commitment to Clean Energy: Apple announced that all data centers, are powered by 100% 
renewable energy. using solar, wind, and other renewable sources. 
• Amazon Web Services (AWS) Wind Farms: for its large network of data centers, AWS announced its 
plans to harness power from sources such as wind farms.    
 
III. 
RESEARCH METHODOLOGY    
In this section, the proposed model depends on using renewable energy (solar panels) to power a data center 
of 100 traditional server with its auxiliary networking and other physical infrastructure like cooling and 
power system. In addition to use an ON/OFF switching technology to switch OFF the idle servers for energy 
saving in case of there is a shortage in power delivered by the batteries especially at night. Fig. 1, illustrates 
a structure for the internal infrastructure of the data center. The analysis of this model passes through three 
phases: Data Center Power Consumption Model, Solar Energy System, and Battery and storage Model. 
 
 
Phase. 1: Data Center Power Consumption Model 
 
The energy consumed by a data center can be divided into two parts: energy used by IT equipment (servers, 
networks,.) and that are used by non-IT equipment facilities (e.g., cooling system, other infrastructures), 
see Fig. 2.

Phase. 2: Solar Energy System 
Solar power is generated when the sunlight is transformed into power. Solar energy is not available during 
the night [8]. The radiation graph of sun in Mosul city for one day (see Fig. 5) is taken into account in the

While energy storage is important as a backup source of electricity, it enables more flexible use of

V. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORKS 
In this paper, we studied the potential of using renewable energy sources for data center implemented using 
of 100 traditional servers and other physical infrastructures and provided with 5 estimated batteries 
according to the energy provided by solar energy system. This paper is provided a model to analyze the 
renewable energy produced by 613 solar panel of size (6.5ft × 3.25ft) each contains 72 solar cell installed 
on an area of 1200m2 in Mosul city to provide 2.967MWh for the total energy load of the data center.  
Because of the variation of the solar power production on a daily and seasonally basis, we propose an 
ON/OFF technology for energy efficient use of the solar power by switching OFF the idle servers in data 
center in case of there is a shortage in solar energy production especially during the night. The results show 
that to run only 4 batteries at night, the data center needs to switch OFF 65% until 90% of the total number 
of servers and consolidating the traffic to the 35% to 10% of the active servers to preserve power usage. 
On the other hand, solar power in a data center in addition to providing power and reducing the air pollution. 
It can increase the sustainability of power system, if the power is generated locally for a limited period, for 
example when power grid is not available, solar power increases the reliability of power system alongside 
the UPS and generators. The integration between different types power management technologies with 
different forms of renewable energy sources in the future will improve the sustainability and reduce the 
pollution of electricity production and enhance the energy efficiency.

Abstract 
This report summarizes the development and demonstration of the three features developed for 
the DOE project “Improving Data Center Energy Efficiency through End-to-End Cooling 
Modeling and Optimization” (Award No. DE-EE0007688). The development of the three software 
features, Feature 1: Optimization of Cooling System Operation, Feature 2: Optimization of 
Airflow Management System, and Feature 3: Simultaneous Optimization of Airflow Management 
and Cooling Systems, are described first. Feature 1 is implemented in Phase 1 of the project and 
demonstrates 15% energy savings from cooling system optimization by applying the proposed 
retrofit solutions. Feature 2 is implemented in Phase 2 and the assessments show cooling energy-
saving potential between 19.3% and 54.0%, depending on the energy-saving measures employed. 
In addition, investigating the energy saving potential for a hypothetical simple data center shows 
about 6.8% energy savings by optimizing the server load placement. Feature 3 is implemented in 
Phase 3 and the results show energy savings of 53.4% and 74.6% for the two partner data centers, 
respectively, compared to the baselines defined in Phase 1. Lastly, the project outcomes including 
software releases and publications are discussed.

1 Introduction 
Data centers house a large amount of mission-critical IT equipment, such as IT servers, 
network and communication servers, and data storage devices, which effectively dissipate their 
input power as heat during operation. The data centers require cooling systems to remove the heat 
dissipation from IT equipment to ensure the IT equipment operates reliably. It was reported that 
data centers consumed approximately 1.8% of the total U.S. electricity [1], among which 24%-
60% are consumed by the cooling system [2]. As the IT equipment becomes increasingly more 
power-intensive, it imposes more challenges on the data center cooling system [3]. As of today, 
air cooling is still the dominant method of primary heat removal, though liquid cooling is emerging 
as an energy-saving alternative.  
The air-cooling system in a medium or large-size data center typically features a raised-floor 
plenum, which is used to distribute the cool air from the cooling equipment, i.e. Computer Room 
Air Handlers (CRAH) or Computer Room Air Conditioners (CRAC) to the racks. Perforated tiles 
deliver the airflow from the plenum to the inlet of the racks. The cool air is then drawn through 
the servers populating the racks, and exhausts at a higher temperature. Sometimes, physical 
containment of the hot or cold aisle is employed to avoid the mixing of the cold air and exhaust 
hot air. 
Model-based design and operation can be adopted to optimize such airflow in data centers. The 
model can help eliminate or reduce over-cooling, while still providing enough cooling to avoid hot 
spots (locations at the intake of IT equipment where the measured temperature is greater than the 
recommended value). For example, in the design phase, the model can help determine the open-
area-ratio and location of the perforated tiles and the depth of the raised-floor plenum. In the 
operation phase, the model can help determine the best supply airflow rate and temperature 
setpoints to achieve optimal energy efficiency. 
In Phase 1 of the project, we developed the software Feature 1 Optimization of Cooling System 
Operation. Using the software Feature 1, we proposed different retrofit solutions to improve the 
energy efficiency of the cooling system for the two partner data centers, which resulted in more 
than 15% energy savings. However, the study only focused on the energy efficiency of the cooling 
system, which may lead to local optima. For example, we did not consider saving energy from the 
AHUs fans, although they are the largest energy consumers in the cooling system for the subject 
data center. The reason is that changing the flowrate of the supply air will have a huge impact on 
the airflow and the thermal performance in the data center room. Without detailed airflow models, 
it is hard to provide any useful suggestions on how to retrofit the fans. 
In Phase 2 of the project, we developed the software Feature 2 Optimization of Airflow 
Management System. Using the software Feature 2, we proposed different retrofit solutions to 

3 
 
improve the airflow and thermal management for the two partner data centers, which also resulted 
in more than 15% energy savings. However, the study only focused on the airflow and thermal 
management, which does not consider the whole problem. For example, we did not consider saving 
energy from raising the supply air temperature. This is because it is very hard to evaluate the 
energy consumption without a detailed cooling system model since different setpoints of supply 
air temperature may lead to different cooling mode. 
To obtain the global optima from simultaneously considering airflow management and cooling 
systems, this report introduces the Feature 3: Simultaneous Optimization of Airflow Management 
and Cooling Systems, which couples the Modelica model for the cooling systems with a self-
learning regression ISAT-FFD model for the airflow management.  
This report is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the development of the software 
Feature 1: Optimization of Cooling System Operation. Then, the software Feature 2: Optimization 
of Airflow Management System is introduced in Section 3 and Feature 3: Simultaneous 
Optimization of Airflow Management and Cooling Systems is described in Section 4. Finally, 
Section 5 summarizes the outcomes of this project.

2 Optimization of Cooling System Operation 
2.1 Data Center Package in Modelica Buildings Library 
2.1.1 Two Commonly Used Cooling Systems for Data Centers 
This data center package includes two commonly used cooling systems for data centers: chilled 
water systems with WSEs, and DX system with ASEs. 
2.1.1.1 Chilled Water System with WSEs 
A commonly used cooling system in data centers is the chilled water system with differently 
configured WSEs. The WSE can be integrated, meaning the economizer can meet all or some of 
the load while the chiller meets the rest of the load, or nonintegrated, meaning the economizer can 
only operate when it can meet the entire load. A brief survey shows that the chiller plant with 
WSEs usually have the following configurations: integrated WSEs on the load side of the common 
leg in a primary-only chilled water system (Figure 1(a)), integrated WSEs on the plant side of the 
common leg in a primary-only chilled water system (Figure 1(b)), integrated WSEs on the load 
side of the common leg in a primary-secondary chilled water system (Figure 1(c)), and 
nonintegrated WSEs (Figure 1(d)) that can be installed in both a primary-only and  a primary-
secondary system.  
Figure 1(a) shows an integrated WSE in a primary-only chilled water system. The WSE is in 
series with the chillers on the chilled water return side and in parallel with the chillers on the 
condenser water side. The WSE is located on the load side of the common leg, which allows the 
WSE to see the warmest return chilled water from the Computer Room Air Handlers (CRAHs) 
and thus maximizes the hours when the WSE can operate. This is also the reason why the WSE on 
the load side is more efficient than that on the plant side (Figure 1(b)). 
Figure 1(d) shows a primary-secondary system with a non-integrated WSE. The WSE is in 
parallel with chillers on both the chilled and condenser water side. The non-integrated WSE should 
be shut off if it cannot meet the entire cooling load. Otherwise, when the chillers and nonintegrated 
WSE work simultaneously, the supply chilled water will be a blend of the cold water leaving the 
evaporators and the relatively warm water leaving the WSEs, and possibly exceed the chilled water 
temperature setpoint.

2.1.2 Data Center Package in Modelica Buildings Library 
The data center package is released in the MBL 5.0.0. and contains component models for the 
abovementioned two commonly used cooling systems in data centers.  This package has the same 
class hierarchy as the MBL and contains various reusable base classes. These base classes together 
with the inheritance and instantiation in the object-oriented modeling language Modelica facilitate 
modeling and simulation of data center cooling systems. 
2.1.2.1 Chilled Water System Models with WSEs  
2.1.2.1.1 General Description 
A group of identical chillers and pumps can be modeled by vectorizing existing chiller and 
pump models, respectively. The vectorized equipment model is assigned with the same design 
parameters but different performance curves if needed. The pseudo-code of vectorization of 
chillers in Modelica is shown in Figure 3. First, a partial class of the chiller model is instantiated 
through vectorization with a number n by specifying the length of the array chiller, which can be 
redeclared with a detailed chiller model later. Line 3 specifies the medium used in the chillers. 
Line 4 defines the identical design parameters for the identical chillers with the keyword “each” 
in Modelica, such as the design capacity. Line 5 defines the performance curves of each chiller by 
obtaining different curves from a performance curve array. The same instantiation method is also 
used to model a group of pumps. In addition, we add isolation valves in the vectorized models to 
avoid circulating flow among components.

The CRAH model is created using existing component models in the MBL with control logics 
added. The CRAH consists of a cooling coil model, an electric reheater model, a steam humidifier 
model, and a variable speed fan model. The control logic is designed to avoid simultaneously 
heating and cooling in the CRAH. 
The WSE model is built on a heat exchanger model with constant effectiveness, and a three-
way valve model. The three-way valve is on the chilled water side and can be adjusted to control 
the chilled water supply temperature by a built-in PID controller. The three-way valve and the PID 
controller can be activated or deactivated based on user’s needs. For example, if the chilled water 
supply temperature at the downstream of the WSE is controlled by regulating the speed of cooling 
tower fans in free cooling, then the three-way valve and the built-in PID controller should be 
deactivated. The switch between activation and deactivation is implemented using a Boolean 
parameter. 
2.1.2.2 Detailed Models: WSE Configurations 
This package implements four different configurations of a chiller plant with WSEs, whose 
schematic drawings are shown in the dashed boxes in Figure 1. 
The chiller plant with integrated WSEs (Figure 1(a)~(c)) can operate in three modes: Free 
Cooling (FC) mode when only WSEs are enabled for cooling, Partial Mechanical Cooling (PMC) 
mode when the chillers and WSEs are both triggered, and Fully Mechanical Cooling (FMC) mode 
when only the chillers are activated. The transition among each cooling mode is achieved by 
manipulating the associated isolation valves. For example, in Figure 1(a), when the cooling system 
is in the FC mode, the isolation valves V1 and V2 in chillers, and V5 for bypassing the WSE are 
shut off.  The isolation valves V3 and V4 in WSEs, and V6 for bypassing the chillers are fully 
opened so that the chilled water can flow through the WSE, and then be delivered by the primary 
pumps to the CRAHs. In the PMC mode, V1~V4 are fully open, V5 and V6 are shut off. In the 
FMC mode, while V3, V4 and V6 are shut off, V1, V2 and V5 are fully open to deliver the chilled 
water through the primary pumps, chillers, and then CRAHs. 
The chiller plant with nonintegrated WSEs (Figure 1(d)) only have the FC mode and FMC 
mode. In the FC mode, the WSE is on and the isolation valves V3 and V4 are fully open, while 

8 
 
the chillers and the associated valves V1 and V2 are off. As opposite to the FC mode, the FMC 
mode requires that the chillers and their associated valves be open.  
2.1.2.3 DX System Models with ASEs  
One major component in the DX system is CRAC. Air-cooled CRAC and water-cooled CRAC 
with single speed, multiple speed or variable speed compressors are modeled using the DX coil 
model located in Fluid.HeatExchanger.DXCoil. These models are based on performance curves, 
and detailed formulas can be found in the reference [4].  
2.1.2.4 Validation 
Each component is verified in a simulation example, following the conventions of the MBL 
mentioned in Wetter, Zuo [5]. Due to the class hierarchy in the MBL and the object-oriented 
language Modelica, we built the data center package based on the base classes and ready-to-use 
component models in the MBL. We validated the data center package using comparative testing 
and analytical verification, which has also been used to validate all individual component models 
in the MBL.  For example, comparative testing is used to validate the water-cooled CRAC model, 
which compares the simulation results of Modelica with EnergyPlus. The WSE model is validated 
by analytical verification, which compares its results with analytical solutions that are derived for 
certain steady-state or transient boundary conditions. 
2.1.3 Examples 
To demonstrate this package, we analyzed two cooling systems for a data center. One is a 
primary-only chilled water system with an integrated WSE on the load side, and the other is a DX 
cooled system with an ASE. We then compared the system performances of the two different 
designs. 
2.1.3.1 System Models 
The data center, located in a dry and cold climate zone, has a design cooling load of 1000 kW, 
but operates at a 50%-part-load condition. Two cooling systems are designed to provide cooling 
for the data center: System 1 is a primary-only chilled water system with an integrated WSE on 
the load side of the common leg (Figure 1(a)), and System 2 is a DX cooled system with an ASE 
(Figure 2).  
The data center room is modelled using a mixed air volume with a heat source. The heat 
transfers and air infiltration through envelope are neglected because they are insignificant 
compared with the heat generated by the computers. No humidifiers are activated in both systems.

2.1.3.2.3 Supply Air Conditions 
Figure 8 shows the scatter plot of the temperature and relative humidity (RH) of the supply air 
leaving the cooling coils in each cooling mode for both systems. The supply air temperature in 
System 1 and System 2 can be controlled at round its setpoint of 18℃, but the RH varies in a 
different range. 
The supply air temperature can be controlled at 18℃ during the PMC and FMC mode in both 
systems, but slightly loses control in the FC mode, wherein the supply air temperature varies 
between 18℃ and 19℃. 
The loss of control of the supply air temperature in the FC mode in both systems is temporary, 
which is caused by the waiting time in the cooling mode controller (Figure 4 and Figure 5). Take 

15 
 
the System 2 as an example. If the OA dry-bulb temperature suddenly increases to the supply air 
temperature setpoint of 18℃ at the moment when the cooling system works in the FC mode and 
the CRAC has been switched off for less than 20 minutes, then the cooling system will still work 
in the FC mode rather than switch to the PMC mode. Hence, the supply air temperature will be 
greater than 18℃ for a while until the fire condition for switching from the FC mode to the PMC 
mode in Figure 5 is satisfied. 
The RH in System 1 varies within the range of 50% to 90%, while that in System 2 fluctuates 
from around 5% to 85% during the whole year.  The reason is that the ASE in the System 2 
frequently introduces the dry outdoor air to the data center room, which contributes to the humidity 
disturbance.

2.1.3.3 Discussions 
This package has the following advantages: first, it can inherit the advantages of the Modelica 
language and MBL. Modelica-based modeling platforms provide some important features such as 

16 
 
object-oriented, and acausal modeling, and support a rich library of numerical solvers for Ordinary 
Differential Equation, and Differential Algebraic Equation systems. MBL provides several 
associated tools to support an automated workflow, coupled simulation with legacy building 
simulation programs, or connections to hardware [5]. 
Second, it supports fast modeling of the chilled water and DX cooling systems in the data 
center. This package is built on the MBL, which provides a rich library of base and ready-to-use 
HVAC equipment models. Besides that, we have added different configuration models of the 
chiller plant with WSEs, which can be used to quickly build a system-level model using the drag 
& drop. 
Third, it supports the analysis of dynamic processes in the cooling and its control system. 
Through the analysis of the control, we can identify deficiencies of the control system.  For 
example, in System 1, the transition conditions in terms of dry-bulb temperature and wet-bulb 
temperature do not have a clear boundary for the FC mode and PMC mode (Figure 7). When the 
OA wet-bulb temperature and the dry-bulb temperature are both in the range of 0℃ to 10℃, the 
system can operate in both the FC and PMC mode for a long time. It means that the system 
sometimes is controlled to run in the PFC mode when it could run in the FC mode, which hence 
does not maximally utilize the cold outdoor air to cool the data centers. 
However, currently only a few system configurations have been implemented. For other 
configurations, users need to assemble system models component-wise by instantiating, through 
drag & drop modeling, components of mechanical equipment and control blocks, and connect 
them to form a system model. 
2.1.4 Summary 
To support fast modeling of cooling systems in data centers, we implemented in the MBL a 
data center package that contains major component models for chilled water plants and direct 
expansion cooling systems. This package has been shown to be able to perform detailed analysis 
of cooling systems in terms of energy efficiency as well as control evaluations for data centers. In 
the next two sections, we apply this package to the cooling systems for a data center located in 
Massachusetts. 
2.2 Case Studies  
Two data centers in the United States were studied for this project: one located in Florida and 
one in Massachusetts. The Florida data center has a raised-floor architecture and uses five 
computer room air conditioners (CRACs) for cooling. The HVAC system primarily uses a chilled 
water-cooling system with a DX system as backup cooling. The Massachusetts data center has a 
raised floor architecture and utilizes a chilled water-cooling system with air-side economizer.  

17 
 
In this report, we only show the detailed results for the Massachusetts data center as an 
example. In this case study, we use the data center package in the MBL to simulate the cooling 
system of a data center in Massachusetts. The details of the subject cooling system and how the 
models are built in Modelica are introduced in Section 2.2.1. In Section 2.2.2, we discuss the 
calibration process and results of the cooling system modeling for the data center in Massachusetts. 
In Section 2.2.3, we propose four retrofit options to save cooling energy, and the energy saving 
potentials are analyzed by combing those four retrofit techniques. 
2.2.1 HVAC System 
2.2.1.1 System Description 
In this section, we summarize all the necessary design information of the data center in 
Massachusetts for modeling and simulation. The information includes the data center room 
(Section 2.2.1.1.1), including IT processing equipment and network devices, and HVAC cooling 
system (Section 2.2.1.1.2).  
2.2.1.1.1 Description of the Data Center 
The Layout of the subject data center room is shown in Figure 9. The data center is a single-
room of 687 m2, containing 138 IT racks and 12 floor-mounted PDUs that collectively consume 
316 kW. The white space is 30.5 m wide and 22.6 m long, with a ceiling height of 3.35 m.  
The data center has a conventional cold-aisle and hot-aisle configuration. The front face of 
each rack orients toward a cold aisle. Each cold aisle is supplied with cold air from perforated floor 
tiles set into a raised floor and fed by an underfloor plenum. The exhaust air from the IT racks is 
directed into open hot aisles and then enters a ceiling plenum through the ceiling tiles. After that, 
the exhaust air will mix with outdoor air in a mixed plenum and then return into the Air Handler 
Unit (AHU). 

18 
 
 
Figure 9 Layout of the subject data center in Massachusetts 
2.2.1.1.2 Description of HVAC system 
The schematic drawing of the HVAC system of the subject data center is shown in Figure 10. 
There are three chillers, chilled water pumps, condenser water pump and cooling towers in the 
schematic drawing, but only two of them run in Lead/Lag configuration and the other one is for 
backup. The chilled water is distributed to the AHU 1 and the AHU 2. The cooling system 
compromises of the following components: 
• 2 chillers which operate in a Lead/Lag configuration 
• 2 variable speed primary chilled water pumps which operate in a Lead/Lag configuration. 
• 2 constant speed condenser water pumps which operates in a Lead/Lag configuration. 
• 2 cooling towers, each tower with a variable frequency driver (VFD) driven fan and basin 
heater which operate in a Lead/Lag configuration 
• 2 AHUs with speed controls based on the static pressure in the plenum

2.2.1.2 System Models 
In this section, we build a system model in Modelica to represent the real cooling system under 
several assumptions. The following paragraph in Section 2.2.1.2.1 discusses these assumptions, 
and then Section 2.2.1.2.2 describes the implementation.  
2.2.1.2.1 Model Assumptions 
• Cooling Load Distribution. The cooling load of the data center mainly comes from the 
heat generated by IT racks. We estimate the cooling load according to the operational data 
at a typical day. The total cooling load of the data center is about 350 kW. We divide the 
data center room into 2 separate and independent zones (assumed to be 175 kW each in 
cooling load). In addition, we assume the load is constant during the simulation period, 
which is reasonable for a data center. 

20 
 
• Cooling System Configuration. Zone 1 and Zone 2 are assumed to be served by AHU 1 
and AHU 2, respectively. The cooling load is addressed either by the chilled water 
generated by chillers or by the outdoor air through the ASEs.  
• Data Center Room. The data center room is modeled as an ideally mixed volume 
implemented in the MBL. The mixed-volume model assumes the air in the data center 
room is completely mixed, which means this model cannot predict the hot spot in the data 
center room. Because we do not need to consider airflow management in the first phase of 
this project, this is a reasonable starting assumption. 
• Underfloor Plenum. We use a resistance model to represent the underfloor plenum, while 
detailed geometry is currently not considered in our Modelica system model. The 
temperature of the underfloor plenum is assumed to be uniform and the temperature rise of 
the supply air from AHUs to the plenum is ignored because of lack of data. In addition, as 
there is no detailed airflow model in our Modelica model, it is difficult to predict the IT 
inlet temperature. Thus, we also assume that the temperature of underfloor plenum is used 
to represent the IT inlet temperature.  
• AHU Fan Walls. In each AHU, there is a fan wall consisting of 12 fans. These fans start 
or stop simultaneously as controlled in the real cooling system. Based on this control logic, 
we use only one fan model to represent the 12 fans.

2.2.1.2.2.2 Local Controls 
Here we summarize the local control strategies for each equipment of the cooling system, 
including the local controls related to AHUs, the chilled water loop, and the condenser water loop. 
AHU Control 
Two identical AHUs are utilized to provide cold air for the data center room. The AHU model 
is a variable volume mixed air unit, with 12 VFD-installed fans, 4 electric heating coils, water 
cooling coils and a steam humidifier. No bypass valves are installed on the waterside of the cooling 
coils. 
The static pressure in the underfloor plenum is controlled at its setpoint of 12.4 Pa by 
modulating the speed of the AHU fans. No staging control is applied to the 12 fans, which means 
the 12 fans start or stop simultaneously. The plenum temperature is controlled at 22.2 ℃ by 
resetting the supply air temperature setpoint in the AHUs within the range of 15.6 ℃ to 22.2 ℃. 
The chilled water supply temperature (CHWST) is reset between 7.8 ℃ and 12.2 ℃ to meet the 
supply air temperature setpoint. When the supply air temperature control signal is smaller than 0.4, 
the CHWST reset is deactivated, and when it is larger than 0.4, the CHWST reset signal will grow 
proportionally between 0 and 1 to reset the CHWST between 7.8 ℃ and 12.2 ℃ (Figure 12). 
The reheater control is also based on the supply air temperature control signal (Figure 12), 
which is generated by the PI controller that is used to control the supply air temperature. When the 
supply air temperature control signal is smaller than 0.4, the reheaters are activated, and if the 
control signal is larger than 0.4, the reheaters are deactivated. 

23 
 
 
Figure 12 Reheater control in the subject data center 
Chilled Water Loop Control 
The chilled water pumps are set up to run one pump per chiller. The speed of the chilled water 
pumps is modulated to maintain a constant pressure difference of 206 kPa between the inlet and 
the outlet of the evaporators. The bypass valve in the common leg is regulated to maintain a 
constant flowrate through the evaporators. 
Condenser Water Loop Control 
The condenser water supply temperature setpoint is reset from 21.1 ℃ to 29.4 ℃ as the wet 
bulb temperature increases from 17.2 ℃ to 25.6 ℃. When the condenser water supply temperature 
rises above the setpoint, the lead cooling tower fan will start and run at the minimum speed. As 
the temperature continues to rise, the fan will modulate toward full speed. The condenser water 
pumps work at constant speed.

The cooling system is modeled using MBL 5.0.1, as shown in Figure 13. The major component 
models include chillers, AHUs, cooling towers, chilled water pumps and condenser water pumps.  
The control system consists of the cooling mode control and controller local controls mentioned

the speed control of the cooling tower fans. The Cooling Mode Control describes the cooling mode 
controller. The differential pressure control and the flowrate control of the evaporators are

2.2.2 Calibration 
To obtain accurate prediction of energy used by the data center cooling system, the Modelica 
models need to be calibrated using real operational data. In this section, we only introduce the 

25 
 
preprocessing procedure of the raw to data used to calibrate the models, and then list the calibration 
results for each component. 
2.2.2.1 Data Preparation 
To improve the calibration results, we need to preprocess the collected measurement data. The 
preprocess consists of two parts: one is a data filter that can filter out the low-quality or undesired 
data, and the other is data separation whereby data is divided into two sets for calibration and 
validation, respectively.  
2.2.2.1.1 Data Filter 
We develop a data filter to detect the low-quality data such as outliers and apply an 
interpolation scheme to approximate the missing measurement data. In addition, we add a new 
feature to the filter by removing undesired information for the purpose of calibration. For example, 
we usually install temperature sensors at the inlet and outlet of the AHUs on both the waterside 
and the airside. These data cannot be used to calibrate the cooling coil models directly because 
sometimes the heating coils are “on” in the AHUs (Figure 14 and Figure 15). Therefore, to calibrate 
the cooling coil model, we need to remove the data which involves reheating. Figure 16 shows the 
filtered data with outliers and undesired data removed to calibrate the cooling coil model.

Since the cooling coil has been used for several years, the heat transfer performance is degraded. 
One metric for thermal performance in a cooling coil is the UA value. The larger the UA value is,

the characteristics of the product, such as dimensions, material, etc. Usually the UA value is known

2.2.3 Optimization 
After calibration, we perform a study to optimize the system to see how much energy could be 
saved for the cooling system in the subject data center in Massachusetts. We first analyze the 
baseline cooling system in terms of control. Then we propose four different retrofit solutions. The 
energy consumption and thermal performance for the combinations of different retrofit solutions 
are analyzed and compared in the end. 

39 
 
2.2.3.1 Baseline system 
The Baseline System uses the calibrated equipment models and the current control settings. 
The results of the calibration and an annual simulation in Modelica shows that there are several 
potential improvements of this system. 
First, as shown in Table 1, the current cooling coils are degraded possibly because of fouling 
after several years’ use. For example, the degraded UA value is 28.6 kW/K in the AHU 1, which 
is only 37% of the design UA value (77.4 kW/K) calculated from manufacture data.  
Second, the cooling system operates either in the Full Mechanical Cooling (FMC) mode or 
Free Cooling (FC) mode; it rarely works in the Partial Mechanical Cooling (PMC) mode, where 
the mixed air is pre-cooled. This is because the transition logic in the baseline cooling mode 
controller is not optimized. As shown in Figure 11, when the outdoor air dry bulb temperature 
𝑇𝑂𝐴,𝑑𝑏 is larger than the supply air temperature setpoint 𝑇𝑆𝐴,𝑓𝑙𝑜𝑜𝑟,𝑠𝑒𝑡 plus a dead band 𝛿𝑇 and the 
dew point temperature 𝑇𝑂𝐴,𝑑𝑝 is higher than a threshold 𝑇𝑂𝐴,𝑑𝑝,𝑙𝑜𝑤, the condition 1 is triggered, 
and the system will transition from the FC mode to the PMC mode. In the Baseline System, the 
𝑇𝑂𝐴,𝑑𝑝,𝑙𝑜𝑤 is set as 12.2 ℃, and the dead band 𝛿𝑇 is 1.1 ℃. However, the system cannot keep 
running in the PMC mode for a long time because the high cutoff limit 𝑇𝑂𝐴,𝑑𝑝,ℎ𝑖𝑔ℎ and the low 
cutoff limit 𝑇𝑂𝐴,𝑑𝑝,𝑙𝑜𝑤 of the dew point temperature are equal, and the dead band temperature 𝛿𝑇 
of 1.1 ℃ is too small. For example, if 𝑇𝑂𝐴,𝑑𝑝 continues increasing to 13.5 ℃, the condition 2 is 
triggered and the cooling system will switch from the PMC mode to the FMC mode. If the outdoor 
air dew point temperature 𝑇𝑂𝐴,𝑑𝑝 decreases to 11.0 ℃, the cooling system will switch from the 
PMC mode back to the FC mode. The dead band for outdoor air dew point temperature is so small 
that it cannot keep the cooling system operating in the PMC mode when 𝑇𝑂𝐴,𝑑𝑝,ℎ𝑖𝑔ℎ equals to 
𝑇𝑂𝐴,𝑑𝑝,𝑙𝑜𝑤.  
Third, there is simultaneous heating and cooling in the AHUs. This is caused by the controls 
for the supply air temperature and the chilled water flowrate. As described in Section 2.2.1.2, the 
supply air temperature setpoint is adjusted to maintain an average temperature of 22.2 ℃ in the 
plenum. To meet the setpoint, the supply air temperature is controlled by resetting the CHWST 
setpoint between 7.8 ℃ and 12.2 ℃, which is determined by a controller with PID control. When 
the PID control output signal is smaller than 0.4, the CHWST reset control will be deactivated, but 
the AHU is still cooling the air. In this case, the electrical reheaters will be turned on to heat the 
supply air to meet the setpoint. As a result, the AHU is simultaneously cooling and heating the air. 
The other problem is that the chilled water flowrate control cannot guarantee that the flowrate of 
the chilled water passing through the cooling coils is as needed. As described in Section 2.2.1.2.2.2, 
the speed of primary pumps is modulated to maintain a fixed pressure difference of 206 kPa 
between the inlet and outlet of the evaporators, and the bypass valve is adjusted to guarantee that 
the chilled water through the evaporators is 0.03 m3/s all the time. Without direct control of the 

40 
 
chilled water through the cooling coils, it possibly leads to a persistent oversupply or undersupply 
of chilled water to the cooling coils. The oversupply of chilled water may over-cool the supply air 
and then trigger reheating to raise the temperature back to the setpoint.  
Fourth, the floor air temperature setpoint of 22.2 ℃ may not be optimal. The floor air 
temperature setpoint 𝑇𝑓𝑙𝑜𝑜𝑟,𝑠𝑒𝑡 plays an important role in achieving an energy efficient data center. 
The higher the 𝑇𝑓𝑙𝑜𝑜𝑟,𝑠𝑒𝑡 is, the longer time the cooling system will work in the FC mode by 
triggering conditions 1 and 3 in Figure 11, and hence the more energy can be saved from 
mechanical cooling. However, to maintain a high floor air temperature, the supply air temperature 
setpoint also needs to be high, which may activate the electrical reheaters in the AHUs and hence 
consume more energy for reheating. Therefore, there is a tradeoff between the energy savings from 
the mechanical cooling and the extra reheating energy by employing a high floor air temperature 
setpoint. An optimization study needs to be conducted to study this tradeoff and find an optimal 
floor air temperature setpoint as discussed in Section 2.2.3.3.5. 
2.2.3.2 Retrofit Solutions 
Based on the analysis of the baseline system, we propose four retrofit solutions:  
• cleaning the cooling coils in the AHUs to increase the heat transfer efficiency;  
• improving the cooling mode controller by increasing the high cutoff limit of the dew point 
temperature in the cooling mode controller;  
• installing a two-way valve on the waterside of the cooling coils and regulate it to control 
the supply air temperature; 
• identifying an optimal floor air temperature setpoint for the cooling system.

2.2.3.3.1 System 1 
In the System 1, we propose to clean the cooling coils. As described in Section 2.2.2.2, the 
current cooling coils are degraded possibly because of fouling. For example, the degraded UA 
value is 28.6 kW/K in the AHU 1, while the design UA value is about 77.4 kW/K, which can be 
calculated from manufacture data (Table 1). Here we assume cooling coils can be fully cleaned so 
that the design UA value is used for each cooling coil. All the controls in the System 1 are the 
same as the Baseline System. 
The simulation results show that cleaning the cooling coil alone actually results in 76% more 
energy consumption than the Baseline System (Table 6). The current supply air temperature 
controls and the reheater control cannot take advantage of more-thermally-efficient cooling coils.  
After being cleaned, the heat transfer effectiveness of the cooling coils increases, which means 
under the same chilled water supply temperature, the cleaned cooling coils can cool the supply air 
to a lower temperature than the degraded cooling coils. As a result, the AHUs with clean cooling 
coils need more reheating to maintain the same supply air temperature than the AHUs with 
degraded cooling coils. For example, to maintain the floor temperature at 22.2 ℃, the supply air 
temperature setpoint is reset between 15.6 ℃ and 22.2 ℃, and hence the CHWST is reset between 
7.8 ℃ and 12.2 ℃ to maintain the supply air temperature. When the supply air temperature is reset 
as 22.2 ℃, the CHWST can be as high as 12.2 ℃. With degraded cooling coils, the AHUs can 
cool the supply air to around 21.0 ℃, and then reheat it to 22.2 ℃. However, with clean cooling 
coils, the AHUs can cool the supply air to around 18.0 ℃, and then reheat it to 22.2 ℃, which 
obviously will consume more reheating energy than the AHUs with degraded cooling coils. What 
is more, in the System 1, the energy of chillers and cooling towers are also increased because the 
heat generated by electric reheaters increases the cooling load of the chillers and cooling towers. 

43 
 
 
Figure 35 Energy consumption of the Baseline System and System 1 
Although reheaters are not big energy consumers in the Baseline System, the simultaneous 
cooling and reheating in an AHU can be avoided by better designing the controller that activates 
and deactivates the reheaters. A common way is to regulate the chilled water flowrate passing 
through the cooling coil by using a two-way or three-way valve. However, just installing extra 
valves on the waterside of the cooling coil is not enough. The control logic also needs to be 
improved to consider the control of the valve position and the differential pressure through cooling 
coils. This technique will be investigated in Section 2.2.3.3.3 ~ Section 2.2.3.3.5. 
In summary, cleaning the cooling coils without changing the supply air temperature control is 
not an efficient solution to the current cooling system in the subject data center.

Comparison of Relative Humidity  
Increasing the high cutoff limit of the dew point temperature in the cooling mode controller 
might pose challenges to the humidity control of the indoor air. With a higher dew point cutoff 
limit, it is easier to introduce humid air to the plenum, in which the mixed air possibly exceeds the 
upper bound of controlled relative humidity (RH). We compare the annual RH in the underfloor 
plenum with the allowable bounds of the current control system (30~85%) in a boxplot. The blue 
dashed line in Figure 40 represents the lower and upper bounds of the RH.  
We can see that by increasing the high cutoff limit of the dew point temperature from 12.2 ℃ 
to 15.2 ℃, the highest RH in the System 2 is higher than that in the Baseline System and exceed 
the upper bound of 85%. The reason is that the cooling system in the subject data center has very 
limited capacity for dehumidification. Cooling coils are the only equipment used to dehumidify 
the supply air. However, the design Sensible Heat Ratio of the cooling coils are 0.99 (688 kW/696 
kW), which means 99% of the heat removed from the cooling coil is sensible heat and only 1% is 
potential heat from dehumidification in design conditions. Thus, when the humid air is introduced 
into the mixers in the AHUs, the cooling coils possibly cannot provide enough dehumidification. 
To reduce the RH in the plenum, three approaches can further be considered:  
• installing independent dehumidifiers in the AHUs and activating them when the RH in the 
plenum is high;  

48 
 
• setting a lower high cutoff limit of the dew point temperature, which can control the RH 
within bounds but save less energy; 
• increasing the floor air temperature setpoint, because the RH decreases as the dry bulb 
temperature increases when the dew point temperature is the same. This method is 
demonstrated in Section 2.2.3.3.5. 
 
Figure 40 Boxplots of the RH in the Baseline system and System 2 
In summary, increasing the high cutoff limit of the dew point temperature to 15.2 ℃ in the 
cooling mode controller saves about 9.2% of energy consumed by the cooling system. However, 
with a high cutoff limit of the dew point temperature, the cooling system introduces more humid 
air to the plenum and possibly compromises the humidity control.  
2.2.3.3.3 System 3 
To overcome the simultaneous heating and cooling in the subject data center, we propose to 
add a two-way valve on the waterside of each AHU and improve the local controls. Instead of 
maintaining a constant differential pressure between the inlet and outlet of the evaporators, the 
System 3 adjusts the speed of primary pumps to maintain a fixed differential pressure of 83 kPa 
between the inlet and the outlet of the cooling coils. This can guarantee that an appropriate amount 
of chilled water passes through the cooling coils. Also, the supply air temperature is controlled by 
adjusting the waterside valve instead of resetting the chilled water supply temperature.

2.2.3.4 Summary 
We conduct a detailed analysis of the Baseline System through an annual simulation in 
Modelica. Several major drawbacks are found in the current cooling system and its control system. 
First, the current cooling coils are degraded possibly because of fouling. Second, the baseline 
cooling mode controller has a narrow-switching dead band of the dew point temperature, which 
prevents the cooling system from operating in the PMC mode for long durations. Third, the 
reheater control system cannot avoid simultaneously heating and cooling in the AHUs. Fourth, the 
floor air temperature setpoint of 22.2 ℃ in current cooling system may not be optimal. 

55 
 
Then, to overcome these drawbacks and explore the energy saving potentials for the cooling 
system, we propose four different retrofit solutions and combine them into the following 7 different 
scenarios.  
• In System 1, we propose to clean the cooling coils in the AHUs. However, the System 1 
consumes 76% more energy than the Baseline System. We conclude that cleaning cooling 
coils cannot save energy if the local controls are not changed.  
• In System 2, we propose to improve the cooling mode controller in the Baseline System. 
By increasing the high cutoff limit of dew point temperature to 15.2 ℃, the cooling system 
saves 9.2% of energy with the penalty of losing control of the RH in the plenum.  
• In System 3, we propose to add a two-way valve on the waterside of the cooling coils in 
the Baseline System to avoid simultaneous heating and cooling in the AHUs. The 
simulation results show that the reheating can be eliminated by regulating the proposed 
two-way valve, which saves about 9.6% of energy compared with the Baseline System.  
• In System 4, we further apply the improved cooling mode controller to the System 3 and 
save 16.9% of energy compared with the Baseline System. 
• In System 5, we propose three potential optimal cooling systems for the subject data center: 
System 5_1 that utilizes an optimal 𝑇𝑓𝑙𝑜𝑜𝑟,𝑠𝑒𝑡 of 25.1 ℃ in the Baseline System, System 
5_2 that utilizes an optimal 𝑇𝑓𝑙𝑜𝑜𝑟,𝑠𝑒𝑡 of 25.1 ℃ in the System 2, and System 5_3 that uses 
an optimal 𝑇𝑓𝑙𝑜𝑜𝑟,𝑠𝑒𝑡 of 27 ℃ in the System 4. Compared with the Baseline System, the 
System 5_1, System 5_2 and System 5_3 can save 4.7%, 14.8% and 24.4% of the total 
energy consumed by the cooling system. The floor air temperature is still within the range 
recommended by ASHRAE for most time of the year, although 𝑇𝑓𝑙𝑜𝑜𝑟,𝑠𝑒𝑡 is high. What is 
more, the relative humidity in the underfloor plenum is also within the desired range in all 
three optimal systems. 
In summary, the floor air temperature setpoint of the current cooling system is near optimal. 
By utilizing the optimal floor air temperature setpoint of 25.1 ℃, we can only get 4.7% energy 
savings. By improving the cooling mode controller, and using the optimal floor air temperature, 
the system can save 14.8% of energy without compromising the floor air temperature and relative 
humidity. To achieve more savings, we change the configuration of the chilled water system by 
adding a two-way valve on the waterside of the cooling coils. The maximum energy savings for 
the proposed configurations can be as high as 24.4% for one year (about $10,900 estimated based 
on $0.1/kWh). 
2.2.4 Summary of Case Studies 
In the case study of the Massachusetts data center, we first give a brief introduction of the 
configurations of the HVAC system and how these models are implemented in Modelica. We then 
calibrate the baseline system using measurement data. The analysis of the calibrated baseline 
system shows that the current cooling system and its controls have several drawbacks: First, the 

56 
 
current cooling coils are degraded possibly because of fouling. Second, the baseline cooling mode 
controller has a narrow switching dead band for the dew point temperature, which prevents the 
cooling system from operating in the PMC mode for long durations. Third, the control of the 
reheaters cannot avoid simultaneous heating and cooling in the AHUs. Fourth, the floor air 
temperature setpoint of 22.2 ℃ in current cooling system may not be optimal.  
To improve the current cooling system and its control, we propose four retrofit solutions: 
cleaning the cooling coils, improving the cooling mode controller, adding a two-way valve on the 
waterside of the cooling coils, and optimizing the floor air temperature. The analysis on the 
proposed techniques shows that the floor air temperature setpoint of the current cooling system is 
near optimal. By utilizing the optimal floor air temperature setpoint of 25.1 ℃, we can only get 
4.7% of energy savings. By improving the cooling mode controller, and using the optimal floor air 
temperature, we can save 14.8% of energy without compromising the floor air temperature and 
relative humidity. To achieve more savings, we can change the configuration of the chilled water 
system by adding a two-way valve on the waterside of the cooling coils. The maximum energy 
savings for the changed configuration can be as high as 24.4% for one year (about $10,900 
estimated based on $0.1/kWh). 
A similar case study was conducted for the Florida data center. In this study, we compare three 
retrofit techniques to save energy in the subject data center, and conclude that cleaning the fouled 
cooling coil alone can save as much as 58% energy of the current cooling system, while only 
increasing the return air temperature setpoint to 25°C instead of 22.8°C can also save about 4% 
energy at no additional cost. To achieve additional energy savings through further increases in the 
return air temperature setpoint, the cooling coils must be cleaned to improve thermal performance 
in the data center in Florida. 
2.3 Summary of Section 2 
In this report, we first give a brief introduction of the data center package we built in the MBL. 
This package contains major component models for chilled water plants and direct expansion 
cooling systems. This package has been shown to be able to perform detailed analysis of cooling 
systems in terms of energy efficiency as well as control evaluations for data centers. 
Then the data center package in MBL is used to do case studies of the cooling systems in two 
data centers located in Florida and Massachusetts, respectively. For each case study, we first 
introduce the configurations of the HVAC system and how these models are implemented in 
Modelica. We then calibrate the baseline system using measurement data. Base on the simulation 
results of the baseline systems, we propose different retrofit solutions for different cooling systems. 
By applying the proposed retrofit solutions, both data centers can save more than 15% energy from

3 Improving Air Flow Management of Data Centers Based on Fast 
Fluid Dynamics and In Situ Adaptive Tabulation 
3.1 Fast Simulation of Data Center Airflow 
When the open-area-ratio of perforated floor tiles is large (e.g., greater than 56%), the airflow 
in the floor plenum and the white space will significantly affect one another. In that case, it is 
preferred to model the plenum and the white space simultaneously. Conversely, when perforated-
tile open-area ratios are small, the spaces are largely decoupled, and it is reasonable to model them 
separately as we do here in this report. The two reference data centers currently employ perforated 
tiles with 25%-open-area. The detailed description of the reference data center will be covered in 
Section 3.2.1. 
In the rest of this section, we first discuss the FFD modeling of data centers. This includes the 
fundamentals shared by traditional CFD and FFD, and some data-center-specific modeling 
considerations.  
3.1.1 Fast Fluid Dynamics

3.1.2.1 Fundamentals of ISAT 
In situ adaptive tabulation (ISAT) is a storage and retrieval algorithm to approximate nonlinear 
functions, which was originally proposed by Pope [21] to accelerate turbulent combustion 
simulations. The idea of ISAT is to dynamically establish a lookup table, based on which a new 
query can be quickly evaluated by local linear regressions [21].   
Generally, let us assume a nonlinear function to be approximated in ISAT as:

where 𝑥 is a real vector space with n linearly independent variables, and 𝑦 is a real vector space 
with p dependent variables. The dimensions of the vector spaces 𝑥 and 𝑦 are determined by the 
numbers of inputs and outputs, which are set by the user. When a new query is available, ISAT 
will first determine the nearest record to the query point. Each record in the ISAT table contains 
the values of 𝑥, 𝑦, mapping gradient matrix, and Ellipsoid of Accuracy (EOA), which will be 
discussed later. EOA refers to a space around the record, in which ISAT deems that an 
approximation (linear interpolation) can be performed “confidently”, which means the error of the 
approximation is within the user-defined threshold. The workflow of the ISAT algorithm is

3.1.2.2 Optimization platform ISAT-FFD-GA  
In the current study, we implemented the ISAT-FFD model, in which ISAT was trained offline 
by running FFD simulations in rapid succession. After ISAT was fully populated (trained), 
optimization studies based on it can be performed. To enable the automatic execution of the ISAT 
training and optimization, we further develop an optimization platform, namely, ISAT-FFD-GA, 
by linking ISAT-FFD with a genetic algorithm [22]. The genetic algorithm is a conventional 
optimization algorithm, in which the candidate solutions (also called individuals) are generated 
and improved after several iterations (also called generations). In each generation, all candidate 
solutions will be evaluated by fitness function and selected (selection). The candidate solutions 
with better fitness value have more possibilities to be inherited by candidate solutions in the next

The workflow of the ISAT-FFD-GA platform is depicted in Figure 49. First, the ISAT table 
will be pre-trained by running FFD simulations to fully populate the queries from pre-defined 
training domains. Then, the genetic algorithm starts the optimization process, in which the fitness 
function (objective function) is evaluated by calling the ISAT-FFD algorithm. Based on the output 
of the fitness function evaluation, the genetic algorithm updates candidate solutions accordingly. 
When evaluating the candidate solution, a fully trained ISAT table should be able to answer mostly 
using the retrieve action, which is instantaneous. In rare cases, when retrieve is deemed by ISAT 
to be inaccurate, a direct call of FFD is executed. After the genetic algorithm converges (in few 
iterations), it outputs the optimal solutions.

3.2 Case Study 1: Airflow Modeling in a Real Data Center 
Like Section 2, two data centers in the United States were studied for this project: one located 
in Florida and one in Massachusetts, but only detailed results for the Massachusetts data center are 
shown in this report. In Section 2, we employed the data center package in the Modelica Buildings 
library to simulate the cooling system assuming that the airflow in the white space was fully mixed. 
In the current study, we use FFD to investigate the cooling performance of the Massachusetts (MA) 
data center by studying the airflow and temperature distributions. First, we validate the use of FFD 
in this context by comparing it to both traditional CFD and experimental measurements. We then 
use FFD simulation to assess and demonstrate additional energy-savings measures that could be 
employed in the MA data center.  
3.2.1 Description of the Reference Data Center 
As shown in Figure 50, the total white space floor area of the data center is approximately 
7,400 ft2. The ceiling is approximately 11 ft above the raised floor. Total power consumption by 
the 151 racks and 12 PDUs is approximately 344 kW. Racks G11 and G13 (i.e., the 11th and 12th 
cabinets in Row G) are empty. A central Air Handling Unit (AHU) supplies cooling airflow 
through the short sides of the plenum, which is supported using 7/8” stanchions.  The airflow is 
then supplied to the IT equipment through 183 25%-open-area tiles (each 2 ft by 2 ft).  The heated 
airflow returns to the CRAH through a dropped ceiling plenum with 42 approximately-83%-open-
area tiles.  For detailed information of the room and its contents, refer to Section 2.

3.2.2 Validation of FFD 
On-site measurements were made in the MA data center to validate the FFD simulations. 
FFD and a commercial CFD program, FloVENT [23], were used to model the data center. It is 
noteworthy that the commercial CFD simulations were performed as “steady state” whereas the 
FFD simulations are inherently transient though run until steady-state conditions were 
reasonably achieved. As stated in Section 3.1, the floor plenum and white space were modeled 
separately.  The floor plenum model produced the tile airflow rates and the white space model 
produced the rack-inlet temperatures.  Note that, in both the CFD and FFD white space models, 
the measured perforated-tile airflow rates and temperatures were prescribed as boundary 
conditions.  
3.2.2.1 Experimental Measurements 
The assessment of the MA data center was performed March 9, 2018 and the assessment of 
the FL data center was performed on June 13-14, 2017. The on-site measurement data consists of 
two parts: the input data and the validation data. The input data is used to set the parameters in the 
FFD and CFD models, and the validation data is used to assess the accuracy of the FFD and CFD 
predictions. The main input data includes the physical dimensions of the room and its contents; 
equipment power estimates; and cooling airflow rates and supply temperatures. The validation 
data includes perforated tile airflow rates and rack inlet temperatures. For detailed information of 
the measurements, refer to Section 2. 
3.2.2.2 Numerical Simulation  
Table 7 summarizes the simulation settings in FFD and CFD. Both used structured grids for 
the simulation of plenum and white space, which are modelled separately. The CFD simulations 
were steady-state while the FFD simulations were transient-state (with a time step size of 0.1 s and 
simulation time of 100 s). The CFD simulation used a 𝑘−𝜀 turbulence model while FFD used a 
zero-equation turbulence model [24]. The CFD simulation was performed on a single core of an 
Intel (R) Xeon (R) CPU E3-1220 v6 processor running on a Windows workstation with of 32 GB 
of RAM. The FFD simulation was performed on an NVIDIA Quadro P2000 GPU on the same 
workstation. We performed grid-independence studies and found that the grid size presented in 7 
is sufficient to generate grid-independent results. Results show that the speedup of FFD over CFD 
is up to approximately 5-100 times.

It is noteworthy that the good performance of FFD and CFD is not surprising, as the flow in 
the plenum should be generally uniform, due to various reasons. First, all 183 tiles are low-open-
area (25%), which reduces tile-to-tile variations. Second, the inflow enters the plenum fairly 
uniformly through the vertical inlet bays and multiple openings on the sides of the plenum. This 
creates, in the plenum, a nearly “plug flow” pattern that is less challenging to model. Third, the 
flow resistance imparted by the raised-floor stanchions further reduce the variations of airflow in 
the plenum. However, we can still observe discrepancies between simulation and measurement at 
few tiles.  One possible explanation is that the tile-airflow measurements were carried out over a 
period of hours yet the period of natural variation of airflow from the cooling system is much 
shorter.  It was not possible to obtain an instantaneous and self-consistent set of tile-airflow 
measurements.

affect the airflow rate and temperature at perforated tiles. In MA data center, the cooling system 
was in free cooling mode, in which the machinal cooling system was not used. The outdoor 
conditions and the control system, however, may still make the temperatures at perforated tiles 
vary. Second, the compact “black-box” modeling of racks does not comprehend the potential 
recirculation of hot air under and through other openings within the rack from the hot to the cold 
aisle. For example, few racks in the MA data center were not fully populated and a few switches 
and other IT equipment have airflow in the reverse direction – from rear to front. We did also 
compare the current CFD results presented here with those in which the racks were modeled down 
to the server-by-server level; we found that, at least, a marginal improvement can be made by 
employing greater rack detail. Finally, and possibly, most importantly, the power and airflow of 
each rack had to be estimated based on rack IT population and power measurements from PDUs 
which served many racks.  In other words, individual-rack power consumption was crudely 
estimated.  The rack airflow was, in turn, crudely estimated assuming 125 cfm of airflow for each 
kW of power dissipation. 
3.2.3 Proposal and Verification of Energy-saving Measures 
We first propose two energy-saving measures for the MA data center to reduce the cooling 
energy consumption. These include adding rigorously sealed cold-aisle containment and adding 
perforated tiles or adjusting the open-area-ratio of the perforated tiles. Then, we quantify the 
energy-saving potential of these measures using FFD or FFD-related methods. 
3.2.3.1 Energy-Saving Measures 
1) Add rigorously sealed containment on cold aisle 
Theoretically, either cold-aisle containment or hot-aisle containment can be utilized to drive 
down the total supply airflow rate. The containment can prevent the mixing of cold air from the 
plenum and warm IT exhaust air. Thus, assuming no leakage, the temperature at the rack inlet will 
be the same as that at the cooling supply. Currently, the MA data center features fully open cold 
and hot aisles. Also, the leakage paths (due to missing blanking panels, odd shaped IT, “backward-
airflow IT”, etc.) in some racks may also lead to the mixing of warm exhaust air with cold supply 
air. 
Therefore, we propose to add rigorously sealed cold-aisle containment and sealing other 
potential leakage paths through and around the racks. Cold-aisle containment is preferred over the 
hot-aisle containment in the MA data center as existing cable trays located over the hot aisles 
complicate their direct ducting to the ceiling plenum.  The major advantage of this energy-saving 
measure is to eliminate the need to supply more airflow than directly consumed by IT equipment. 
In the MA data center, the air-ratio, defined as the ratio of supply airflow to the IT airflow, can be, 
theoretically, reduced to 1 from its current value of 2.2; This directly results in a reduction of fan 

73 
 
power consumption. The detailed description of this energy-saving measure is summarized as Case 
1 in Table 10. 
2) Add new perforated tiles and change %-open area of others 
From Figure 52, we can identify the racks with high inlet temperatures, such as E17 and E18. 
These temperatures almost approach 80.6 F (27 °C), which is the ASHRAE recommended limit 
for the IT equipment to operate reliably. If we do nothing other than decrease the total supply 
airflow rate, the inlet temperatures at those racks will clearly exceed the threshold.  
Therefore, we propose to first add few perforated tiles and increase the open-area-ratio of other 
existing perforated tiles near the racks with high inlet temperatures, and then decrease the total 
supply airflow rate. The validated FFD model can be used to identify the maximum temperature 
and its compliance with the ASHRAE threshold value. The detailed description of this energy-
saving measure is summarized as Case 2 in Table 10.

As summarized in Figure 55, adding rigorously sealed cold-aisle containment leads to the 54%

contrast, the rigorous cold-aisle containment and sealing of Case 1 provides a better efficiency 
improvement and will generally not require ongoing experimental audits or modeling to preserve 
the initial savings.

3.3.1 Description of the Reference Data Center 
The whitespace is 22 ft (6.7m), 18 ft (5.5m), 12 ft (3.7m) in length, width, and height, 
respectively. The total whitespace floor area of the reference data center is 396 ft2 (36.8 m2) and 
the layout is shown in Figure 56. The data center includes 10 racks consuming a total of 60 kW. 
The ceiling is 12 ft (3.7 m) above the raised floor in this area. The CRAC supplies airflow to the 
uncontained cold aisle through the raised-floor plenum and 10 25%-open-area perforated tiles. 
Cool airflow is drawn into the racks, heated, and expelled into the hot aisles. The airflow in the 
hot aisles then returns to the CRAC directly through the room without a ceiling plenum. We note 
that this hypothetical data center is proposed to represent the airflow physics in typical data centers 
based on raised-floor architecture. 
The total workload is 60 kW, which is evenly distributed over 10 racks in the baseline. The IT 
airflow is estimated as the product of the total IT power and the ratio IT airflow to IT power 
dissipation, which is assumed to be 125 cfm/kW (212 m3/h/kW). The total supply airflow rate is 
7500 cfm (12,750 m3/h), which is identical to the cooling airflow rate needed by the racks.

Settings of FFD Simulations: 
For modeling simplicity/convenience, we make the following simplifications. First, only 
whitespace is modeled, and the underfloor plenum is excluded. Since all the perforated tiles in this 
case are 20% open-area, to model the whitespace, or, under-floor plenum in a detached way is 
justifiable, as the airflows in the two spaces are fairly separated [30].  Second, we employ a black-
box rack model and therefore workload is shifted at the rack level. For the detailed description of 
the rack model, refer to [31]. 
As recommended by VanGilder and Zhang [32], FFD simulation adopts a uniform 6 inches 
(0.15 m) grid, which leads to a total 38,016 cells. Since FFD simulations are inherently transient; 
we use a time step size of 0.1 s and simulation time of 200 s to reach steady-state conditions. FFD 
employs a zero-equation turbulence model [24]. The FFD simulation was performed on a 
workstation with 4 Intel(R) Xeon(R) E5-1603 CPUs and an AMD FirePro W8100 GPU and the 
results of initial tests showed that the time cost for each simulation is about 61 s. 
Training of ISAT-FFD Models: 
From sensitivity analysis, we found that the IT power of the racks located at the ends of the 
rows have relatively more influence on the overall maximum rack-inlet temperature. Therefore, 
we determined to use two inputs in the ISAT model describing the IT power of the racks at the 
row ends. We assume the powers of Rack-1 and Rack-6 are always the same (represented by Input 
1) and the powers of Rack-5 and Rack-10 are always the same (represented by Input 2). For other 
racks, we assume the remaining IT power is uniformly distributed to the 6 racks in the middle of 
the rows. We note that making these assumptions is to reduce the number of inputs for the ISAT 
such that the training cost is reasonable. 

82 
 
We proposed three cases with predefined total error tolerances: 0.2, 0.4, and 0.6 for case 1-1, 
1-2, and 1-3, respectively. The two inputs range from 1.0 kW to 10.0 kW. The output is the 
maximum rack-inlet temperature for the 10 racks.  
The results of the three cases are shown in Table 15. In Case 1-1, the total number of queries 
used in the training is 255,497, in which 99.3% are retrieve actions, 0.6% are grow actions and 
0.1% are add actions. In Case 1-2 and Case 1-3, the total numbers of queries drastically dropped 
to 15,630 and 4,190. Consequently, the numbers of the retrieve, grow and add actions are also 
significantly decreased. As a result, the training process takes 34.7 hours for Case 1-1, and only 
3.8 hours and 1.8 hours for Case 1-2 and Case 1-3.

3.3.4 Summary 
In this report, we proposed a simple hypothetical data center example to assess the feasibility 
of applying ISAT-FFD-GA to optimize the IT load distribution to save cooling energy. Three cases 
with different user-defined error tolerances were studied. With an error tolerance of 0.4 oC, the 
training of ISAT required 3.8 hours and the optimization required an additional 0.1 hours. The 
total time cost of 3.9 hours is acceptable in terms of performing design optimization, though this 
is a small-scale application with additional simplifying assumptions. A 6.8% energy savings can 
be achieved relative to the baseline by optimizing IT load placement without any physical 
equipment moves or changes. We finally note that, for ISAT-FFD to be utilized in the real-time 
optimizations of control settings for real data centers, further speedup would be required.

3.4 Summary of Section 3 
We first introduce the development of FFD to simulate the airflow and temperature of data 
center plenum and whitespace. FFD is then validated with two real data centers. The predictions 
from FFD are acceptable compared to CFD results and experimental measurements. FFD achieves 
some 5-100 times of speedup compared to CFD with the two reference data centers. Finally, we 
demonstrate how FFD helps evaluate and improve the airflow management for data centers. Two 
energy-saving measures including adding containment and adding perforated tiles or adjusting 
open-area-ratio of perforated tiles, have been proposed for each data center. It has been found that 
energy savings of at least 19.3% and 47.0% can be obtained for the two reference data centers, 
respectively. We also demonstrate the optimization platform, ISAT-FFD-GA, with a hypothetical 
simple data center and find that the energy saving potential for the reference case is about 6.8% by 
optimizing the server load placement. 
In this report, we focus on the modeling and improvement of the airflow management for data 
centers. We also evaluate the energy savings through a rough estimate without simulating the 
cooling system model. However, the changes of the airflow or temperature distribution may affect 
the performance of the cooling systems. Also, the interaction between the cooling system and 
airflow and temperature distribution in data centers may be dynamical, which makes it even harder 
to consider the effect of the two studied domains influenced by each other.

and Cooling Systems in Data Centers 
The previous sections introduced Feature 1: Flexible Models of Cooling System and Feature

4.1.1 Introduction of Data Center Airflow Management and Cooling Systems 
 
Figure 60 Airflow pattern and cooling systems in a typical raised-floor data center 
Figure 60 shows the configuration and airflow pattern in a typical raised-floor data center. The 
raised-floor plenum and perforated tiles at each cold aisle are designed to uniformly distribute the 
cold air to each cold aisle. The white space in the data center (space allocated for IT equipment) is 
partitioned into cold aisles and hot aisles by rows of racks. The cold air from the cooling system 
is supplied to the cold aisle, then flows through the IT racks and carries heat dissipation from IT 
equipment, then exhausts to the hot aisle and returns to the cooling system through the ceiling 
plenum. Improving the design of the cold and hot aisles can help the airflow management goal of 
ensuring a low rack inlet temperature (not exceeding 27 oC according to ASHRAE [33]) by 
mitigating the mix of cold air and hot air. 
The cooling system configures a chilled water system with airside economizers (ASEs), which 
operate in three cooling modes: (1) free cooling (FC) mode, where only ASEs are activated; (2) 
partial mechanical cooling (PMC) mode, where the chilled water system and ASEs work 
simultaneously; (3) fully mechanical cooling (FMC) mode, where only the chilled water system is 

88 
 
used. The transition conditions between different cooling modes are determined by the weather 
data and system settings and conditions.

In Phase 3 of the project, we couple the self-learning regression ISAT model with the Modelica 
model for cooling systems. Figure 62 shows the proposed coupling scheme of building energy 
simulation (BES) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) models. The existing coupling scheme 
exchanges data between two programs that perform transient simulations. Such a coupling scheme 
has been used in the literature to perform optimization studies, such as optimal thermostat 
placement in an office room using typical outdoor conditions for a single day [34]. The bottleneck 
of this scheme is that the high computational demand of CFD simulations makes it difficult to be 
used in real-time optimal operation or long-term applications such as annual energy simulations. 
We propose a new coupling scheme to accelerate the CFD simulations by integrating an online 
self-learning regression model, which is a storage and retrieve algorithm trained with results of 
CFD simulations during the simulation process.

4.2.2 Case 4-1: Coupled Simulation 
4.2.2.1 Model Implementation 
According to ASHRAE thermal guidelines for data centers [33], the IT equipment air inlets 
should be established as the common measurement point for temperature and relative humidity 
compliance. However, the cooling system model built in Phase 1 is not capable of predicting the 
rack inlet temperatures since a it adopts a well-mixed room, which assumes the temperature is 
uniformly distributed within the room. In this case, we implement the ISAT-FFD model to predict 
the maximum rack inlet temperature and include it to the cooling system model built in Phase 1. 
 
Figure 66 The implementation of the ISAT-FFD model in Modelica 
The implementation of the ISAT-FFD model is shown in Figure 66. There are two inputs: 
supply air flowrate and temperature, and one output to predict the maximum rack inlet temperature. 
To train the ISAT model, the FFD model for the MA data center is simulated, which was developed 
and validated in Section 3. The error tolerance for the training of the ISAT-FFD model is defined 
as 0.2 oC. The time interval to exchange data between the Modelica model and ISAT-FFD model 
is 400s.

We first introduce the development of the coupled Modelica and ISAT-FFD model. Then, we 
demonstrate the model with three cases for each of the two reference data centers. In the first case, 
an ISAT-FFD model is implemented to predict the maximum rack inlet temperature with supply 
air flowrate and temperature as inputs. The second case extends the first case with a feedback 
control loop and the results show that the maximum rack inlet temperature is controlled at the 
target value. In the third case, the supply flowrate is optimized to achieve a minimum energy 
consumption while meeting the thermal requirements of data centers regarding the maximum rack 
inlet temperature, from which 53.4% and 74.6% of energy savings are achieved compared to the 
baseline for the FL and MA data centers, respectively. 
 
 
 

104 
 
5 Project Outcomes and Future Work 
5.1 Open Source Software Releases 
Several open-source software packages developed for this project have been released publicly. 
The Modelica models for data center cooling systems were released in the Modelica Buildings 
library (V5.0.0) and can be found at the following link:  
https://simulationresearch.lbl.gov/modelica/releases/latest/help/Buildings_Applications.html#Bui
ldings.Applications. The coupled ISAT-FFD models are in the development repository of the 
Modelica Buildings library: https://github.com/lbl-srg/modelica-buildings,  and will be released in 
the future. The self-learning ISAT-FFD models for data center airflow are also available on the 
project website: https://www.colorado.edu/lab/sbs/doe-datacenter.  
5.2 Commercialization and Industry Impact 
Project contributor Schneider Electric plans to release software applications by the end of 2020 
or early 2021 based on the Fast Fluid Dynamics (FFD) model developed and extended to data 
center applications under the current DOE-sponsored project.  These include:  
• EcoStream: This is an airflow-modeling software tool used by Schneider Electric 
employees and sales partners to help customers design adequately cooled and efficient 
facilities.  EcoStream focuses exclusively on cooling modeling and performance and is 
“product agnostic”, i.e., it is not tied to Schneider Electric or product brands.  
• EcoStruxure IT Advisor: This is a commercial software product used for designing and 
managing existing data centers.  It helps manage IT assets, cooling systems, environmental 
sensors, etc. as well as providing airflow-modeling capabilities.  For more information, see 
https://ecostruxureit.com/ecostruxure-it-advisor/.     
• ISX Designer: Like EcoStream, ISX Designer is a software tool used by Schneider Electric 
employees and sales partners.  However, ISX Designer is a product configurator and sales 
tool with which users can create a complete 3D model of a data center comprised of 
Schneider Electric equipment.  The airflow-modeling capability ensures that the cooling 
system will function as intended.  
The new FFD-based CFD engine for all of the above tools will run remotely in the cloud and 
on GPUs rather than traditional CPUs.  This allows Schneider Electric to provide the accuracy of 
commercial CFD while preserving the speed and scalability of more simplistic CFD models. All 
of the tools listed above have existed for years but relied on airflow-modeling capabilities of a 
simplistic potential-flow CFD model or algebraic model.  By adopting the new FFD-based CFD 
model, Schneider Electric expects to increase the accuracy and breadth of its software applications 
and service offerings.  At the highest level, Schneider intends to make commercial-CFD-grade 

105 
 
capabilities accessible to a large class of data center designers and operators who previously found 
the technology too expensive, too difficult to use, or too slow. 
Another key industrial impact as an outcome of this project is a Massachusetts data center 
investing over $100,000 to retrofit their data center based on results from this project. 
5.3 Publications and Presentations 
The work completed for this project has led to eight journal publications, four conference 
papers and two completed Ph.D. theses, which are listed in the following sections. These 
publications have also been deposited to the DOE website https://www.osti.gov/. In addition, more 
journal papers are in progress based on work from this project. Lastly, eight presentations at 
conferences hosted by ASHRAE, IBPSA, IEEE and more have been delivered as an outcome of 
this project.

5.4 Future Work 
Based on our current research, we propose the following directions for future research. First, a

training methods and error tolerances in the ISAT model. Next, the training efficiency of the ISAT

such as smart control of natural ventilation.
