A Reinforcement learning-Based GWO-RNN approach for Energy Efficiency 
in Data Centers by Minimizing Virtual Machine Migration 
Parsa Parsafar1 
1: Department of Engineering, University of Mazandaran, Babolsar, Iran 
Address: Iran,  Mazandaran province, Amol city 
Phone Number: +989117468277 
Fax Number: Not applicable 
Email address: p.parsafar08@umail.umz.ac.ir 
 
Abstract 
In the era of exponential data growth, data centers play a critical role in providing reliable and efficient 
computing resources. However, the energy consumption of these facilities has become a significant 
concern, driving the need for innovative solutions to enhance energy efficiency. This paper presents a novel 
approach to minimizing virtual machine (VM) migrations in data centers, thereby reducing energy 
consumption. Our model leverages a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) optimized with a Grey Wolf 
Optimizer (GWO) to predict energy consumption and preemptively manage workloads. By incorporating 
this RNN, our model effectively anticipates the energy consumption of future, leading to make the best 
decision to migrate the VM or not. Furthermore, energy consumption is monitored in real-time to identify 
overloading and underloading of VMs. The reinforcement GWO-RNN framework adapts dynamically to 
changing workloads, ensuring optimal resource allocation and reducing the frequency of energy-intensive 
VM migrations. Experimental results demonstrate a significant reduction in energy consumption and 
improved efficiency in data center operations, showcasing the potential of this approach for sustainable 
computing. 
Keywords: Data Center, Energy Efficiency, Recurrent Neural Networks, Virtual Machine Migration, Grey 
Wolf Optimizer, Reinforcement Learning 
1. Introduction 
As the backbone of modern digital infrastructure, data centers are indispensable in supporting a vast array 
of online services and applications [1]. The burgeoning demand for computational power has led to an 
unprecedented rise in the number and size of data centers worldwide. Consequently, energy consumption 
in these facilities has escalated, raising environmental and economic concerns. One of the primary 
contributors to energy inefficiency in data centers is the frequent migration of VMs, which is often 
necessary to balance loads and maintain performance but incurs significant energy costs. 
The challenge lies in developing a predictive and adaptive system that minimizes unnecessary VM 
migrations while ensuring optimal resource utilization and maintaining service quality. Traditional 
approaches to VM management often rely on static thresholds and reactive policies, which are insufficient 
in handling dynamic and complex data center environments. There is a critical need for a more sophisticated 
solution that can foresee potential bottlenecks and preemptively manage workloads. 
This paper introduces a pioneering approach to address these challenges by integrating a RNN with a GWO. 
The RNN-GWO model is designed to predict future resource utilization patterns based on a comprehensive 
set of inputs, including temporal factors (day of the week, week of the month, minute of the hour, hour of 
the day), application usage statistics, resource utilization metrics (CPU, network, I/O, memory), and the 

number of active sessions. The GWO algorithm optimizes the RNN’s learning process, enhancing its ability 
to accurately predict potential bottlenecks and make informed decisions about VM migrations. 
The primary objectives of this study encompass several key aims. Firstly, the study seeks to develop a 
predictive model that enhances data center efficiency by minimizing VM migrations. This model aims to 
achieve this through accurate forecasting of resource utilization and proactive identification of potential 
bottlenecks within the system. Secondly, the study aims to optimize the neural network training process by 
leveraging the GWO. This optimization effort targets improving the predictive accuracy and overall 
efficiency of the model, thereby enhancing its practical applicability in data center operations. Finally, the 
study endeavors to evaluate the efficacy of the proposed RNN-GWO model in reducing energy 
consumption and optimizing operational efficiency within data centers. 
This paper makes several significant contributions to the field. Firstly, it introduces a novel integration of 
RNN and the GWO for predictive workload management in data centers. This integration represents an 
innovative approach towards achieving efficient resource allocation and workload balancing. Secondly, the 
paper proposes a methodology that reduces energy consumption through the minimization of VM 
migrations, thereby contributing to sustainable data center practices. Lastly, comprehensive experimental 
validation showcases the effectiveness of the proposed model in real-world data center environments, 
affirming its potential for practical implementation and operational enhancement. 
2. Research Background 
The Data centers, which provide critical infrastructure for computing and storage, have become essential 
to the modern digital ecosystem. However, this unprecedented expansion comes with significant challenges, 
particularly concerning energy consumption [2]. Data centers are notoriously energy-intensive, with 
operational efficiency and environmental impact being major concerns for both stakeholders and the wider 
community. 
 
Fig. 1. A non-live VM migration procedure overview. 
VM migrations, while necessary for load balancing and performance optimization, often lead to substantial 
energy expenditures. This is because moving VMs incurs overheads related to data transfer, system 
reconfiguration, and additional computational demands. Consequently, reducing the frequency of these 
migrations without compromising the performance and reliability of the data center becomes a critical goal. 

Traditional methods for VM management have typically relied on static policies and thresholds [3, 4]. These 
approaches are reactive rather than proactive, often resulting in inefficiencies that exacerbate energy 
consumption. They lack the adaptability needed to handle the dynamic nature of data center workloads, 
which can vary widely based on numerous factors such as time of day, application demands, and overall 
resource utilization. 
In 2018, Zhou and colleagues, proposed an approach named EEOM, which addressed the growing energy 
consumption issues in large-scale data centers, which have been escalating by over 15% annually, leading 
to significant environmental and financial impacts [5]. The study highlights that traditional VM migration 
strategies often rely on single resource factors such as CPU utilization, and the proposed approach optimizes 
VM migration by simultaneously considering both CPU and memory factors. The paper presents an 
enhanced VM migration framework that refines three critical aspects: the timing of migration triggers, the 
selection of VMs for migration, and the choice of host servers for migrated VMs. This refined approach 
aims to improve energy efficiency by reducing unnecessary migrations and minimizing overall energy 
consumption, as validated by experimental results. The study’s reliance on specific threshold parameters 
for energy and SLA violations might limit its adaptability to different types of workloads or varying 
operational conditions. More adaptive or dynamic threshold settings could improve performance across 
diverse scenarios. Furthermore, while the paper addresses both memory and CPU utilization, this 
consideration may be insufficient for real-world data center scenarios. A comprehensive analysis should 
also include other critical resources such as storage I/O and network bandwidth to ensure a more realistic 
and effective approach.  
Later, in 2020, a proposal method introduced an Energy Efficient Strategy (EES) for VM consolidation in 
cloud environments, aiming to enhance energy efficiency while maintaining performance standards [6]. It 
started with a power model where server power consumption is expressed as a function of CPU utilization, 
integrating this function over time to compute total energy consumption. The paper further defines key 
performance metrics, such as SLATAH for SLA violations and PDM for performance degradation due to 
migrations, and combines them into SLAV and ESV metrics to assess overall efficiency. The strategy 
includes algorithms for detecting server overloads and underloads, utilizing thresholds based on the PPR 
for overload detection and dynamic thresholds for underload detection based on cluster-specific CPU 
utilization and server characteristics. As the previous study, this comprehensive study also does not account 
for other crucial resources such as storage I/O and network bandwidth. Furthermore, using the highest PPR 
value among the hosts as the threshold for labeling a server as overloaded is clearly not optimal. A more 
effective formulation for determining this threshold should be developed. Moreover, this study focuses on 
detecting whether a host is overloaded or underloaded in terms of power usage, rather than VMs themselves. 
Consequently, it is necessary to select a VM from all the VMs on that host to migrate, in order to optimize 
the host's consolidation. This process poses a challenge, as it may be difficult to identify the ideal VM to 
migrate to other hosts, adding computational complexity to the proposed model. By thoroughly 
investigating the resource utilization and energy consumption of each VM, the model's accuracy can be 
significantly enhanced. 
In the same year, Jalali and colleagues proposed a method aimed at addressing the high energy consumption 
caused by non-optimized VM migration called CLANFIC [7]. Their approach minimizes VM migration by 
anticipating future energy consumption patterns based on an Adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system 
(ANFIS) model. The main issue with this paper is its lack of clarity. It does not explain how the ANFIS 
model is trained, nor does it specify the inputs and outputs of the ANFIS. More importantly, the paper fails 
to define what is meant by "future" and how far into the future it refers. Moreover, the impact of the model 
on the throughput of the hosts or VMs is not addressed. 

Additionally, a significant gap in the existing studies is the absence of reinforcement learning mechanisms 
to reward or penalize decisions. Consequently, there is no assurance of continuous improvement in these 
studies over time. 
This paper addresses all the gaps identified in previous studies, providing clear explanations and thorough 
evaluations. We ensure transparency in our model's training process and clearly define our metrics and 
future projections. Moreover, our approach demonstrates superior performance in key evaluation metrics 
compared to existing methods. 
3. Methodology 
In this section, we explain the proposed algorithm which tries to minimize the number of migrations in 
VMs. As discussed, VM migrations can lead to SLA violations because of increasing the response time for 
users. Therefore, the number of migrations should be minimized to prevent potential SLA violations and 
reduce the power usage of data centers. 
Anticipating the future is a strategy widely used in various fields, including marketing, finance, and 
technology. This forward-thinking approach allows organizations to make informed decisions that can lead 
to better outcomes. In this context, we propose a novel method utilizing reinforcement learning-based deep 
learning to predict future energy consumption. By accurately forecasting energy usage, our algorithm can 
determine the optimal actions, such as whether to perform a VM migration at crucial moments of VM 
usage. The proposed method leverages advanced neural networks trained on historical data to identify 
patterns and trends in energy consumption. This predictive capability enables the system to make proactive 
decisions, optimizing energy efficiency and resource utilization. At pivotal times, the algorithm evaluates 
the potential benefits and costs of migrating VMs, ensuring that the decision maximizes overall system 
performance and energy savings. To ensure accountability and continuous improvement, all decisions made 
by the algorithm are monitored and reviewed at the end of a specified period, as determined by the system 
management. This review process involves analyzing the outcomes of each decision and assigning rewards 
or penalties based on their effectiveness. By incorporating this feedback loop, the system learns and adapts 
over time, continually enhancing its decision-making capabilities. Fig.2 depicts a comprehensive view of 
the proposal methodology which is discussed in details in upcoming subsections.

Fig. 2. A comprehensive overview of the implementation. 
 
3.1. GWO-RNN 
The integration of GWO with RNNs presents a novel method for minimizing energy consumption in data 
centers. This approach optimizes the process of VM migration by leveraging the historical data of the data 
center to make informed decisions on whether to perform VM migration or not. This section delves into the 
components of the GWO-RNN approach and explains how they work together to enhance predictive 
capabilities and resource management. 
3.1.1. Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO) 
GWO is a nature-inspired optimization algorithm that mimics the leadership hierarchy and hunting 
mechanism of grey wolves in nature [8]. The algorithm categorizes wolves into four groups: alpha, beta, 
delta, and omega, where the alpha wolf leads the hunt, supported by beta and delta wolves, while omega 
wolves follow the leaders. Key Advantages of GWO include: 

• 
Exploration and Exploitation: GWO balances exploration (searching new areas) and exploitation 
(refining known areas) effectively. 
• 
Simple Implementation: GWO is straightforward to implement and requires fewer control 
parameters compared to other optimization algorithms. 
• 
Robust Performance: It performs well across various types of optimization problems, making it 
suitable for complex environments like data centers. 
3.1.2. Long Short Term Memory Recurrent Neural Networks (LSTM-RNN) 
RNNs have recently gained significant popularity across various domains, including natural language 
processing and electric load forecasting, due to their ability to model temporal dependencies in sequential 
data [9]. However, standard RNNs face challenges such as the vanishing and exploding gradient problems, 
which hinder their ability to learn from long data sequences [10]. Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) 
networks address these issues by incorporating additional gates that provide better control over the gradient 
flow within the cell. The structure of an LSTM cell is illustrated in Fig. 3, and its computations at time 𝑡 
are described as follows:

In equation (1), 𝑖, 𝑓 and 𝑜 are input, forget, and output gates, 𝑐 is the cell state and, ℎ is the hidden state. 
Symbol ⊙ represents the elementwise multiplication and 𝜎 is the sigmoid activation function. Input-
hidden and hidden–hidden weights are Wx’s and Wh’s, whereas the corresponding biases are bx’s and bh’s. 
The adoption of LSTM networks in our case study proves to be highly beneficial due to their ability to 
effectively handle long-term dependencies and mitigate the issues associated with vanishing and exploding 
gradients. 
3.2. Model Construction 
This study`s proposal, employs a regression model to predict future energy consumption using historical 
data. This predictive capability is crucial for making informed decisions regarding VM migrations, as it 

allows us to anticipate energy demands and optimize resource allocation. The specific time horizon for 
these predictions and the methodology for determining this are discussed in the following subsections. 
3.2.1. Simulation 
The data used in this study is recorded in CloudSim. CloudSim is a comprehensive simulation framework 
that provides a standardized environment for modeling and simulating cloud computing infrastructures and 
services [11]. It supports a wide range of resource utilization metrics such as CPU utilization, memory 
usage, disk storage usage, the number of active sessions, and application usage. This simulator is 
particularly suitable for academic work because it allows researchers to create controlled, repeatable 
experiments and explore different scenarios without the cost and complexity of real cloud environments. 
By using this simulator, we can ensure the reliability and consistency of our data collection. This historical 
data forms the basis for training our GWO-RNN model, enabling it to learn and predict future resource 
utilization accurately. Additionally, CloudSim's extensibility allows us to integrate custom modules and 
algorithms, making it an ideal tool for developing and testing new approaches in cloud resource 
management. Table 1 contains most important controlling parameters of the simulation in CloudSim:

3.2.2. Model training 
The integration of GWO with RNN aims to enhance the RNN's learning process by optimizing the network's 
parameters, leading to improved predictive accuracy and energy efficiency [12]. GWO optimizes the 
weights and biases of the RNN, replacing traditional gradient descent methods. Furthermore, unlike 
gradient descent, which can get stuck in local minima, GWO's exploration capabilities allow it to find global 
optima, leading to better overall performance. 
The GWO-RNN approach begins with the initialization phase, where a population of grey wolves is 
established with random weights and biases for the RNN, and the initial positions of the alpha, beta, and 
delta wolves are determined. During the prediction phase, the RNN is utilized to forecast future resource 
utilization based on inputs such as CPU utilization, memory usage, disk storage usage, number of active 
sessions, applications' usage, and temporal factors. In the optimization phase, the fitness of each wolf, which 
represents a set of weights and biases, is evaluated based on prediction accuracy and energy consumption. 
The positions of the alpha, beta, and delta wolves are then updated based on the best solutions found, while 

the positions of the remaining omega wolves are adjusted to explore new areas and refine existing solutions. 
This prediction and optimization cycle is repeated until convergence or a specified number of iterations is 
reached. Finally, the optimized RNN is employed for real-time prediction and VM migration decisions, 
ensuring energy-efficient operations in the data center. Fig. 4 illustrates the GWO-RNN workflow in

3.3. Overload and Underload Detection 
The ultimate goal of energy efficiency is to enhance the effectiveness of energy use, requiring hosts to 
accomplish more tasks with less energy. To achieve this, real-time monitoring of VM resource utilization 
is essential for identifying instances of both overloading and underloading. Whenever energy consumption 
exceeds the current overload threshold or falls below the current underload threshold, the GWO-RNN 
model activates to predict future energy utilization within a specified time frame (discussed further in the 
paper) to ensure whether the VM migration is really needed based on future resource utilizations or not. 
These thresholds will be updated during appropriate periods when the data center is not experiencing high 
workload, as desired by the system manager. 
One effective method for detecting these imbalances involves establishing dynamic thresholds for overload 
and underload conditions. Static thresholds are inadequate due to the ever-changing nature of data centers 
and real-world scenarios. Therefore, it is crucial to determine these thresholds dynamically. 
A widely recognized approach for determining dynamic thresholds is the Performance to Power Ratio 
(PPR). PPR actually measures the number of Server Side Java operations completed over a specific period, 
divided by the average active power consumption during that same period. This method provides a practical 
means of setting adaptive thresholds to improve energy efficiency [13].

Pseudo code for threshold determination 
Initialize theta_under and theta_over 
Set learning rate eta

Set maximum iterations max_iter 
 
Function Cost(theta_under, theta_over): 
    SLA_violations = Calculate_SLA_Violations(theta_under, theta_over) 
    energy_consumption = Calculate_Energy_Consumption(theta_under, theta_over) 
    return SLA_violations + 200 * energy_consumption 
 
Function Gradient_Descent(theta_under, theta_over, eta, delta_theta, max_iter): 
    for iteration from 1 to max_iter: 
        cost_current = Cost(theta_under, theta_over) 
         
        # Compute gradient with respect to theta_under 
        theta_under_plus_delta = theta_under + delta_theta 
        cost_under_plus_delta = Cost(theta_under_plus_delta, theta_over) 
        gradient_theta_under = (cost_under_plus_delta - cost_current) / delta_theta 
         
        # Compute gradient with respect to theta_over 
        theta_over_plus_delta = theta_over + delta_theta 
        cost_over_plus_delta = Cost(theta_under, theta_over_plus_delta) 
        gradient_theta_over = (cost_over_plus_delta - cost_current) / delta_theta 
         
        # Update theta_under and theta_over 
        theta_under = theta_under - eta * gradient_theta_under 
        theta_over = theta_over - eta * gradient_theta_over 
         
        # Check for convergence (optional) 
        if abs(gradient_theta_under) < tolerance and abs(gradient_theta_over) < tolerance: 
            break 
    return theta_under, theta_over

4.1. Experimental settings and performance metrics 
To evaluate the performance of this model, we used ApacheBench (ab), a popular HTTP benchmarking 
tool developed by the Apache Software Foundation [22]. ApacheBench is widely used for measuring the 
performance of web servers by generating a large number of requests to the server and recording how it 
handles them. This tool allows us to simulate multiple concurrent users and analyze various metrics such 
as the number of requests per second, the time taken to serve the requests, and the percentage of failed 
requests. By employing ApacheBench as the experiment, clear understanding of how the system performs 
under different loads is obtained. 
In the realm of cloud computing and virtualization, robust metrics are crucial for evaluating system 
performance and ensuring efficient resource management. Metrics like PDM (Performance Degradation 
due to Migration), SLATAH (Service Level Agreement Time-aware Heuristic), and MLU (Maximum Link 
Utilization) play a pivotal role in the comprehensive assessment of virtualization strategies and resource 
management techniques. 
PDM measures the impact of VM migrations on overall system performance. VM migration is 
essential for load balancing and energy efficiency but can introduce performance overheads. By 
quantifying this degradation, PDM provides insights into the trade-offs involved in migration 
decisions. This metric helps in evaluating how migrations affect application performance and 
identifying strategies to minimize negative impacts, balancing the benefits of load distribution 
against the costs of performance hits during migration, and ensuring that service quality remains 
within acceptable bounds. For instance, recent research by Han et al. [23] demonstrated how 
dynamic VM allocation strategies can be optimized by considering PDM to reduce both energy 
consumption and performance penalties. 

On the other hand, SLATAH is used to ensure that resource allocation and management strategies 
adhere to predefined SLAs [24]. It focuses on time-aware decision-making to as it is the most 
obvious indicator for web applications to guarantee that SLA conditions are met. This metric is 
essential for ensuring that cloud services meet their contractual performance guarantees, resource 
allocation efficiency, and anticipating and mitigating potential SLA violations before they occur. 
Additionally, MLU is an essential metric for evaluating network performance in data centers. MLU 
measures the highest level of bandwidth utilization across all network links. High MLU values indicate 
potential bottlenecks and inefficiencies in the network, which can lead to increased latency and reduced 
performance. By monitoring MLU, data center operators can identify and address network congestion 
points, ensuring optimal data flow and improved overall system performance. Recent studies, such as [25], 
have shown that optimizing MLU can significantly enhance network efficiency and reduce latency, thereby 
improving the quality of service (QoS) for end-users.

5. Conclusion 
In this study, we addressed the critical issue of energy consumption in data centers by developing a novel 
approach that minimizes VM migrations. Our proposed model integrates a RNN with a GWO to predict 
and manage workloads preemptively. The results demonstrate significant reductions in energy consumption 
and VM migrations, achieving our primary objective of enhancing data center efficiency. The GWO-RNN 
model dynamically adapts to changing workloads, ensuring optimal resource allocation and reducing the 
energy costs associated with VM migrations. By leveraging the predictive capabilities of RNNs and the 
optimization power of GWO, our approach significantly outperforms traditional methods that rely on static 
thresholds and reactive policies. Our comprehensive evaluation framework, incorporating metrics like 
SLATAH violations and PDM, confirms the model's effectiveness in real-world environments. The 
substantial improvements demonstrated in key performance metrics highlight the potential of our approach 
for practical implementation in data centers. This study contributes to the field of sustainable computing by 
providing a robust solution for reducing energy consumption in data centers, ultimately supporting more 
efficient and environmentally friendly computing infrastructures. The GWO-RNN framework offers a 
promising avenue for future research and development in cloud computing and resource management. 
Looking ahead, incorporating real-time feedback loops and advanced reinforcement learning strategies 
could also improve the adaptability of the model to varying workloads and dynamic data center 
environments.

metadata.name: EVALUATION OF THE USE OF RADIATIVE COOLING TECHNOLOGY TO SUPPORT THE AIR CONDITIONING SYSTEM OF A DATA CENTRE

GD48.full_text:
CYTEF 2024 − XII Congreso Ibérico | X Congreso Iberoamericano de Ciencias y Técnicas del Frío 
Elche, España, 26-28 junio, 2024 
DOI: 10.21134/ck1khq50
EVALUATION OF THE USE OF RADIATIVE COOLING TECHNOLOGY 
TO SUPPORT THE AIR CONDITIONING SYSTEM OF A DATA CENTRE 
Jonathan Cofré-Toledo1, 2, Roger Vilà1, Albert Castell1, Ingrid Martorell1, *
1: Sustainable Energy, Machinery and Buildings (SEMB) Research Group, INSPIRES Research Centre, 
Universitat de Lleida, Pere de Cabrera s/n 25001, Lleida Spain 
2: Departamento de Ingeniería Mecánica, Facultad de Ingeniería, Universidad de Santiago de Chile, Av. 
Libertador Bernardo O’Higgins Nº3363, Estación Central, Santiago 
*E-mail of corresponding author: ingrid.martorell@udl.cat
Abstract: Data centre space cooling systems consume a lot of energy and will increase over the 
years. Therefore, it is necessary to propose new refrigeration strategies. Radiative cooling (RC) 
production is a renewable alternative solution with a promising future. In this work, the energy 
modelling of the air conditioning system of a data centre coupled to a RC emitter is carried out 
to explore the benefits of this technology. The system consists of a water chiller connected to a 
cooling coil through which air is circulated for distribution in the data centre room. The 
simulations were carried out for a typical summer week in Barcelona. The RC production was 
carried out during the night, and this energy was used during the day and was implemented 
directly in the energy balance of the data centre room, considering emission surfaces of 80 and 
60% of the total building roof, reducing the water chiller energy consumption by 13 and 10% 
respectively. In the transient behaviour of the temperature in the data centre room, when the RC 
was used to reduce the peak cooling load, a reduction of the temperatures was observed 
approaching to the design setpoint, therefore, the Information Technology (IT) equipment was 
not affected. 
Keywords: Data Centre, Air Conditioning, Radiative Cooling, Numerical Simulation, Energy Modelling. 

CYTEF 2024 − XII Congreso Ibérico | X Congreso Iberoamericano de las Ciencias y Técnicas del Frío 
Elche, España, 26-28 junio, 2024 
2 
1. INTRODUCCIÓN 
Data centres house the IT equipment used for processing and storage of data, communication, and networking, 
as well as the associated extensive supporting infrastructures to power and cool this equipment. These data 
centres can be as simple as a rack with a server closet or as large as a warehouse and are considered the central 
nervous system of the century [1]. Data centres are the consumers of a large amount of the electric energy in 
the world, due to the power supply and the cooling systems [2]. Data centres consume around 6 billion kWh 
per year [3], which means that they are more than 40 times as energy intensive than any other building [4]. 
The current growth in the number of data centres is increasing this need of electrical demand. Recent trends to 
reduce the environmental impact of data centres involve using renewable energy and/or waste heat utilization 
[5]. Therefore, it is necessary to study renewable cooling supply technologies. A potential alternative to cover 
part of the refrigeration of buildings data centres is the generation of cold through the phenomenon of radiative 
cooling. Wang et al. [6] studied radiative cooling technology for data centre cooling systems, obtaining an 
average annual energy saving of 28%. The literature is not sufficient in the field of data centres and radiative 
cooling, which makes this work promising for the future. In this study, an energy simulation of a data centre 
building was performed using an EnergyPlus template to obtain the cooling loads. Energy modelling of a 
cooling coil and an air-cooled chiller was carried out. The night-time radiative cooling production was 
calculated and incorporated directly into the energy balance of the data centre zone. The energy consumption 
and the transient temperature behaviour in the data centre room were studied. 
2. MATERIALS AND METHODS 
2.1 Simulation of the data centre building 
For the energy simulation, a single-zone data centre template available in the EnergyPlus example files was 
used [7]. The building has a surface of 232 m2 and a height of 4.6 m. The thermal envelope of the building is 
concrete, with a thermal conductivity of 1.7 W/m∙K, a density of 2242.6 kg/m3, and a specific heat of 836.8 
J/kg∙K. The floor has a thickness of 10 cm, and thermal inertia was considered in the simulation, the wall has 
a thermal resistance equal to 2.3 m2∙K/W and the roof equal to 5.5 m2∙K/W. 
The envelope is exposed to solar radiation and wind speed. The energy balance was solved by finite difference 
and the TARP and DOE-2 algorithms were used for internal and external convection heat transfer, respectively. 
The weather file of Barcelona was used, calculating the cooling load for a typical summer week in August, 
from 15th to 21st June. Regarding the load schedule, from 01:00 AM to 06:00 AM it operates at a load fraction 
of 0.5, until 08:00 AM at 0.75, between 08:00 AM and 06:00 PM at 1.0, and until midnight at 0.8. 
In the simulation, it was assumed that all electrical power absorbed by the IT equipment in the data centre is 
completely converted into heat. For the estimation of internal loads, the watts per floor area method was 
considered for lights and direct power method for IT equipment. The internal load of the IT equipment was 
dimensioned using the parameters given by the EnergyPlus simulation template and the recommendations of 
Schneider electric [7] [8]. In the case of a water chiller coupled to an air distribution circuit, with 75% rack 
usage, and considering 100 units of 500 W, the heat dissipation density is approximately 216 W/m2. The result 
of the EnergyPlus simulation of the data centre building are the cooling load (qCL) and the outdoor dry bulb 
and sky temperatures (TDB and Tsky), these temperatures were used to calculate the RC production (qRC). 
2.2 Energy modelling 
The air conditioning system consists of an air-cooled water chiller connected to a cooling coil through which 
air is circulated for distribution in the data centre room, such as a Computer Room Air Handler (CRAH) unit. 
The RC is applied directly in the energy balance of the data centre zone. The maximum night-time RC potential 
is calculated, and it is assumed that a thermal storage system, such as a cold-water tank, will store this energy 
and supply it during the day. Figure 1 shows the operating scheme of the air-conditioning system coupled to 
the direct production of radiative cooling.

The zone temperature (Tz) is designed to be between 18 to 27 °C according to the ASHRAE standard for 
classes A1, A2, A3 and A4 [9]. The mass flow rates in the air (ṁair) and water (ṁwater) loop were sized to 
ensure temperature gradients equal to 10 and 5 °C, respectively. Thermophysical properties were considered 
constant for air and water, respectively. The zone temperature in the data centre room was modelled by energy 
balance using the Equations (1):

The cooling coil was modelled using heat exchanger theory applying the effectiveness-NTU (Number of

The energy model used for the air-cooled water chiller is the Chiller Electric EIR (Energy Input Ratio) based 
on the inlet temperature of the condenser [7] (ambient temperature). The mathematical model consists of the 
calculation of three empirical curves, which consider the behaviour of the chiller at its reference conditions, 
the real input and output energy and the part load ratio. 
Therefore, the calculation procedure for energy modelling is: (1) Calculate the cooling load (qL) for a typical 
summer week in Barcelona, (2) calculate the mass flow rates of air and water using the design thermal gradients 
and the cooling load, (3) the initial zone temperature (Tz) is set at 27°C (upper limit) and the cold-water supply 
temperature is constant equal to 6.67°C (reference condition), (4) calculating all NTU parameters, (5) obtain 
the temperatures Tco and Tsup, (6) obtain the qevap, which is assumed to be equal to the qreal calculated from 
the heat exchange process, (7) calculate all the Chiller Electric EIR parameters using qevap and Tco, (8) 
calculate the new zone temperature using the previous timestep. (9) return to step 4 and repeat the calculations

for all seven days of the week. 
2.3 Radiative cooling calculation 
To produce night-time radiative cooling, a flat plate emitter is assumed, with water as the heat transfer fluid, 
and it is assumed that the emitter surface of the RC will be equivalent to 80% and 60% of the total roof area 
of the data centre building. Also, in this work it is assumed that a thermal storage system, will store this energy 
and supply it during the day. 
The night-time radiative cooling production is carried out from 09:00 PM to 07:00 AM and the cooling supply 
from RC to the data centre will take place between 09:00 AM to 07:00 PM of the next day. 
From an energy balance on the RC surface places on the roof of the data centre building, the radiation emitted 
by the surface minus the infrared radiation coming down from the atmosphere is equal to the net radiative 
cooling power, and using the Stefan-Boltzmann equation, as well as Kirchhoff's law, the RC equation becomes:

the sky temperature in K calculated from the infrared radiation intensity (obtained from the models available 
in EnergyPlus). The RC power is directly incorporated in the energy balance, which has an impact on the 
transient temperature behaviour as well as on the energy consumption of the chiller. The final energy balance

3. ANALYSIS OF RESULTS AND DISCUSSION 
3.1 Energy simulation results 
The outputs of the EnergyPlus simulation of the data centre building are the cooling load, the dry bulb 
temperature, and the sky temperature. The result of the cooling load was used to calculate the design parameters 
in the energy modelling of the cooling coil and the air-cooled chiller. The dry bulb and sky temperature results 
were used to calculate the maximum radiative cooling power. Figure 2 shows the outputs of the energy 
simulation, (a) cooling load, and (b) the dry bulb and sky temperatures. The cooling load results are consistent 
with the schedule load profile defined previously in section 2.1 of data centre simulation.

3.2 Radiative cooling production 
In the calculation of the radiative cooling production, eighty percent (RC80) and sixty percent (RC60) of the 
total roof surface of the data centre building was considered, equivalent to 186 m2 and 139 m2 respectively. 
The total RC energy produced during the night in a typical summer week of Barcelona between 09:00 PM to 
07:00 AM was 942 kWh for the RC80 and 707 kWh for the RC60. The cold supply inside the data centre is 
between 09:00 AM to 07:00 PM. The results of the radiative cooling production for (a) RC80 and (b) RC60 
are presented in Figure 3.

3.3 Chiller electric power and energy consumption 
The effect of the implementation of radiative cooling contributes to the decrease of the electrical power peak 
of the air-cooled chiller. These demand peaks occur during peak hours when electricity is most expensive. So, 
radiative cooling could help reduce electricity costs, as well as energy consumption. The energy consumption 
of the air-cooled chiller decreases by 13% and 10% when RC80 and RC60 are incorporated respectively.

3.4 Temperature behaviour 
The objective of this work is to study the effect of the incorporation of night radiative cooling on the operation 
of a data centre air conditioning system. Therefore, the chiller has a constant cold water supply temperature 
(Tci (To−evap)) equal to 6.67 ºC and was sized for the maximum cooling load. Figure 5 shows the transient 
behaviour of the (a) zone air temperature (Tz) and the (b) supply air temperature (Tsup) in the data centre. 
Incorporating radiative cooling production directly into the energy balance of the data centre zone results in a 
reduction of temperature peaks when the cooling load is higher. Using a setpoint temperature of 24 °C as the 
lower limit and an upper limit of 27 °C, the incorporation of radiative cooling does not affect the design 
temperature range of the IT equipment. Supply air temperatures also decrease at peak cooling loads, this is 
logical considering that the chiller always supplies chilled water at the same temperature and if the data centre 
area experiences a decrease in temperatures due to the addition of radiative cooling it is to be expected that the 
supply temperature will decrease after the heat exchange in the cooling coil.

4. CONCLUSIONS 
An energy simulation of a data centre building was carried out using an EnergyPlus template, considering the 
design parameters recommended by ASHRAE and Schneider electric, to obtain the cooling loads and the dry 
bulb and sky temperatures for a typical summer week in Barcelona. With the cooling load, an air conditioning 
system similar to a Computer Room Air Handler (CRAH) unit was dimensioned. The dry bulb and sky 
temperatures were used to calculate the night-time radiative cooling production considering emission surfaces 
of 80% (RC80) and 60% (RC60) of the total roof area of the data centre building. Energy modelling was 
carried out for a cooling coil and an air-cooled chiller, using effectiveness-NTU method and the Chiller Electric 
EIR based on the inlet temperature of the condenser, respectively. The method of incorporating the cold 
produced by radiative cooling was carried out directly in the energy balance of the data centre zone, obtaining 
the transient behaviour of the temperature in the room. The energy consumption of the air-cooled chiller 
decreases by 13% and 10% when RC80 and RC60 are incorporated respectively. Incorporating radiative 
cooling production directly into the energy balance of the data centre zone results in a reduction of temperature 
peaks when the cooling load is higher and does not affect the design temperature range of the IT equipment.

metadata.name: Data centre water consumption

GD49.full_text:
PERSPECTIVE
OPEN
Data centre water consumption
David Mytton
1✉
The information communication technology sector will experience huge growth over the coming years, with 29.3 billion devices
expected online by 2030, up from 18.4 billion in 2018. To reliably support the online services used by these billions of users, data
centres have been built around the world to provide the millions of servers they contain with access to power, cooling and internet
connectivity. Whilst the energy consumption of these facilities regularly receives mainstream and academic coverage, analysis of
their water consumption is scarce. Data centres consume water directly for cooling, in some cases 57% sourced from potable water,
and indirectly through the water requirements of non-renewable electricity generation. Although in the USA, data centre water
consumption (1.7 billion litres/day) is small compared to total water consumption (1218 billion litres/day), there are issues of
transparency with less than a third of data centre operators measuring water consumption. This paper examines the water
consumption of data centres, the measurement of that consumption, highlights the lack of data available to assess water efﬁciency,
and discusses and where the industry is going in attempts to reduce future consumption.
npj Clean Water (2021) 4:11 ; https://doi.org/10.1038/s41545-021-00101-w
INTRODUCTION
The
information
communication
technology
(ICT)
sector
is
expecting huge growth over the coming years. By 2023, 5.3
billion people will have internet access, up from 3.9 billion in
20151. By then, 29.3 billion devices will be connected to the
internet (up from 18.4 billion in 2018), with access speeds
doubling between 2018 and 2023 to a global average of
110 Mbps1. More people having faster access to online services
means internet trafﬁc will double by 20222.
To reliably serve these billions of users, internet properties rely
on millions of dedicated computers called servers. These servers
are located in data centres, which provide reliable power, cooling
and internet access. Around 40% of servers are in small data
centres3 such as cabinets in an ofﬁce side room, but newer
facilities are increasingly “hyperscale” warehouses, hundreds of
thousands of square meters in size, and run by the big three
cloud vendors (Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud Platform,
Microsoft Azure)4.
The energy consumption of data centres regularly receives
attention in both the academic and mainstream press. Despite the
ICT sector being responsible for some of the largest purchases of
renewable energy5, there remains considerable uncertainty about
total data centre energy consumption. Estimates for 2018 range
from 2006 to 500 TWh7. Some extreme analyses even suggest
energy consumption could quadruple by 20308, whereas other
estimates show energy growth plateauing6. Regardless of the
precise number, data centre energy is an important topic of public
interest. However, it is just one aspect of the environmental
footprint
of
ICT.
A
less
well
understood
factor
is
water
consumption.
Crucial for industry and agriculture, the availability and quality
of water is a growing global concern9. Projections suggest that
water demand will increase by 55% between 2000 and 2050 due
to growth from manufacturing (+400%), thermal power genera-
tion (+140%) and domestic use (+130%)10. ICT is another sector
contributing to that demand.
In Fiscal Year 2018 (FY18), Google reported 15.8 billion litres of
water consumption, up from 11.4 billion litres in FY1711. Similarly
with Microsoft who reported using 3.6 billion litres in FY18, up
from 1.9 billion litres in FY1712 (Fig. 1). Ofﬁces make up some of
this total, but data centres also use water.
This paper examines the water consumption of data centres,
how that consumption is measured by the ICT sector, and
considers where the industry is going in attempts to reduce future
water consumption.
DATA CENTRE WATER USE
Total water consumption in the USA in 2015 was 1218 billion litres
per day, of which thermoelectric power used 503 billion litres,
irrigation used 446 billion litres and 147 billion litres per day went
to supply 87% of the US population with potable water13.
Data centres consume water across two main categories:
indirectly through electricity generation (traditionally thermo-
electric power) and directly through cooling. In 2014, a total of 626
billion litres of water use was attributable to US data centres4. This
is a small proportion in the context of such high national ﬁgures,
however, data centres compete with other users for access to local
resources. A medium-sized data centre (15 megawatts (MW)) uses
as much water as three average-sized hospitals, or more than two
18-hole golf courses14. Some progress has been made with using
recycled and non-potable water, but from the limited ﬁgures
available15 some data centre operators are drawing more than half
of their water from potable sources (Fig. 2). This has been the
source of considerable controversy in areas of water stress and
highlights the importance of understanding how data centres use
water.
This section considers these two categories of data centre water
consumption.
Water use in electricity generation
Water requirements are measured based on withdrawal or
consumption. Consumption refers to water lost (usually through
evaporation), whereas water withdrawal refers to water taken
from a source such as natural surface water, underground water,

Power plants generate heat using fossil fuels such as coal and
gas, or nuclear ﬁssion, to convert water into steam which rotates a
turbine, thereby generating electricity. Water is a key part of this
process, which involves pre-treating the source water to remove
corroding contaminants, and post-treatment to remove brines.
Once heated into steam to rotate the turbine, water is lost through
evaporation, discharged as efﬂuent or recirculated; sometimes all
three16.
The US average water intensity for electricity generation for
2015 was 2.18 litres per kilowatt hour (L/kWh)17, but fuel and
generator technology type have a major impact on cooling water
requirements. For example, a dry air cooling system for a natural

Hydropower systems also use large volumes of water despite
being considered a cleaner source of electricity. Water evaporation
from open reservoirs is a major source of losses, particularly in dry
regions and where water is not pumped back into the reservoir or
passed onto downstream users. The US national average water
consumption for hydropower is 16.8 L/kWh compared to 1.25 L/
kWh for thermoelectricity17.
With the majority of generation still from fossil fuels18, the
transition to renewables is important for both carbon and water
intensity. Only solar and wind energy do not involve water in
generation, yet both still consume water in the manufacturing and
construction processes9. Estimates suggest that by 2030, moving
to wind and solar energy could reduce water withdrawals by 50%
in the UK, 25% in the USA, Germany and Australia and 10% in
India19.
In the data centre sector, Google and Microsoft are leading the
shift to renewables. Between 2010 and 2018, the number of
servers increased 6 times, network trafﬁc increased 10 times and
storage capacity increased by 25 times, yet energy consumption
has only grown by 6%6. A major contributor to this has been the
migration to cloud computing, as of 2020 estimated to be a $236
billion market20 and responsible for managing 40% of servers4.
Due to their size, the cloud providers have been able to invest
in highly efﬁcient operations. Although often criticised as a metric
of efﬁciency21, an indicator of this can be seen through low power
usage effectiveness (PUE) ratios. PUE is a measure of how much of
energy input is used by the ICT equipment as opposed to the data
centre infrastructure such as cooling22, deﬁned as follows:
PUE ¼ Data Centre Total Energy Consumption
ICT Equipment Energy Consumption
(1)
PUE is relevant to understanding indirect water consumption
because it indicates how efﬁcient a particular facility is at its
primary purpose: operating ICT equipment. This includes servers,
networking and storage devices. An ideal PUE of 1.0 would mean
100% of the energy going to power useful services running on the
ICT equipment rather than wasted on cooling, lighting and power
distribution. Water is consumed indirectly through the power
generation, so more efﬁcient use of that power means more
efﬁcient use of water.
Traditional data centres have reported PUEs reducing from 2.23
in 2010 to 1.93 in 20206. In contrast, the largest “hyperscale” cloud
providers report PUEs ranging from 1.25 to 1.18. Some report even
better performance, such as Google with a Q2 2020 ﬂeet wide
trailing 12-month PUE of 1.1023.
As data centre efﬁciency reaches such levels, further gains are
more difﬁcult. This has already started to show up in plateauing
PUE numbers24, which means the expected increase in future
usage may soon be unable to be offset by efﬁciency improve-
ments25. As more equipment is deployed, and more data centres
are needed to house that equipment, energy demand will
increase. If that energy is not sourced from renewables, indirect
water consumption will increase.
Power generation source is therefore a key element in
understanding data centre water consumption, with PUE an
indicator of how efﬁciently that power is used, but it is just the ﬁrst
category. Direct water use is also important—all that equipment
needs cooling, which in some older facilities can consume up to
30% of total data centre energy demand26–28.
Water use in data centre cooling
ICT equipment generates heat and so most devices must have a
mechanism to manage their temperature. Drawing cool air over
hot metal transfers heat energy to that air, which is then pushed
out into the environment. This works because the computer
temperature is usually higher than the surrounding air.
The same process occurs in data centres, just at a larger scale.
ICT equipment is located within a room or hall, heat is ejected
from the equipment via an exhaust and that air is then extracted,
cooled and recirculated. Data centre rooms are designed to
operate within temperature ranges of 20–22 °C, with a lower

There
are
several
different
mechanisms
for
data

cooling27,28, but the general approach involves chillers reducing
air temperature by cooling water—typically to 7–10 °C31—which is
then used as a heat transfer mechanism. Some data centres use
cooling towers where external air travels across a wet media so
the water evaporates. Fans expel the hot, wet air and the cooled
water is recirculated32. Other data centres use adiabatic econo-
misers where water sprayed directly into the air ﬂow, or onto a
heat exchange surface, cools the air entering the data centre33.
With both techniques, the evaporation results in water loss. A
small 1 MW data centre using one of these types of traditional
cooling can use around 25.5 million litres of water per year32.
Cooling the water is the main source of energy consumption.
Raising the chiller water temperature from the usual 7–10 °C to
18–20 °C can reduce expenses by 40% due to the reduced
temperature difference between the water and the air. Costs
depend on the seasonal ambient temperature of the data centre
location. In cooler regions, less cooling is required and instead free
air cooling can draw in cold air from the external environment31.
This also means smaller chillers can be used, reducing capital
expenditure by up to 30%31. Both Google34 and Microsoft35 have
built data centres without chillers, but this is difﬁcult in hot
regions36.
MEASURING DATA CENTRE WATER USE
In the same way that PUE represents data centre energy
consumption, water usage effectiveness (WUE) is a metric for
data centre water consumption37, deﬁned as follows:
WUE ¼ Annual Site Water Usage
ICT Equipment Energy
(2)
The unit is L/kWh. However, this offers a limited view because it
only includes the water consumed on-site. As discussed above,
water from electricity generation is also important for under-
standing the total data centre footprint. A similar metric was
published in the academic literature38, but the industry also
proposed WUEsource at the same time as WUE37, deﬁned as
follows:
WUEsource ¼ Annual Source Energy Water Usage þ Annual Site Water Use
ICT Equipment Energy
(3)
The availability of water intensity factors to calculate annual
source energy water usage is a limitation of this metric. Some
countries publish ﬁgures, such as the US National Renewable
Energy Laboratory39, but there is large variance across and within
technologies40, and they become out of date as the grid
decarbonises41.
This may be one reason why less than a third of data centre
operators track any water metrics and water conservation is
ranked as a low priority32. Facebook is one of the few companies
to report WUE, even publishing real-time online dashboards for
their Lulea42, Forest City43 and Prineville44 data centres. None of
the top three cloud vendors (by usage45) publish water efﬁciency
metrics, although Google11 and Microsoft12 both report total
water consumption (Fig. 1).
CLOUD VENDOR WATER USE
The move to cloud computing is a major reason behind claims
about ﬂattening data centre energy usage over the last few years6.
In the past, organisations had to buy physical equipment and
lease space to deploy it in a data centre. With cloud computing,
those physical resources still exist but are instead owned and
operated by the cloud vendor, and split into virtual units sold by
the second, hour or per user request. This means resources can be
more efﬁciently allocated and the cloud vendors can afford to
spend money on improving efﬁciency that would otherwise not
be worth the cost to companies operating at smaller scale.
However, it also means customers no longer have visibility into
the resource consumption behind their purchases, thereby
making it impossible to assess the environmental impact of their
cloud use46.
Google and Microsoft have started to compete on their
sustainability credentials47 and both have been reporting detailed
environmental metrics for several years (Fig. 1). However, neither
company attributes their water consumption to data centres, and
their ﬁgures only represent direct water usage, ignoring water
used in electricity generation. Breakdowns of water source are
absent, which has proven controversial when they compete for
stressed potable sources.
Google considers water use to be a trade secret and has
engaged in tactics to prevent the release of information about
how it works with local utilities48. In South Carolina, Google has
free access to pump 1.9 million litres per day due to how state
law regulates access to aquifers49. This became controversial
with local residents and conservation groups with an application
to triple the daily volume50 because at the same time the local
utility was asked to reduce its withdrawal by 57% over the
following 4 years48. Google has worked on water conservation
projects in the past51, and is leading the industry on energy
projects such as access to renewable electricity52, so its
aggressive approach to water use seems at odds with its overall
sustainability strategy.
Amazon plans to be carbon neutral by 204053 (Google and
Microsoft achieved this in 2007 and 2012, respectively) and has
lagged behind on when it plans to match all its electricity
consumption with 100% renewables (by 202554). Amazon’s
ecommerce and logistics business mean it has a much larger
environmental footprint, which is not directly comparable with
Google or Microsoft, but it could still break out ﬁgures for its
Amazon Web Services cloud business. Instead it offers only vague
statements about its water consumption55. Meanwhile, Microsoft
announced its intention to replenish more water than it consumes
by 203056. Amazon stands out for its lack of transparency.
ALTERNATIVE WATER SOURCES
Where data centres own and operate the entire facility, there is
more ﬂexibility for exploring alternative sources of water, and
different techniques for keeping ICT equipment cool.
Google’s Hamina data centre in Finland has used sea water for
cooling since it opened in 201157. Using existing pipes from when
the facility was a paper mill, the cold sea water is pumped into
heat exchangers within the data centre. The sea water is kept
separate from the freshwater, which circulates within the heat
exchangers. When expelled, the hot water is mixed with cold sea
water before being returned to the sea58.
Despite Amazon’s poor environmental efforts in comparison to
Google and Microsoft, they are expanding their use of non-
potable water55. Data centre operators have a history of using
drinking water for cooling, and most source their water from
reservoirs because access to rainfall, grey water and surface water
is seen as unreliable32. Digital Realty, a large global data centre
operator, is one of the few companies publishing a water source
breakdown (Fig. 2). Reducing this proportion is important because
the processing and ﬁltering requirements of drinking water
increase the lifecycle energy footprint. The embodied energy in
the manufacturing of any chemicals required for ﬁltering must
also be considered. This increases the overall carbon footprint of a
data centre.
Amazon claims to be the ﬁrst data centre operator approved for
using recycled water for direct evaporative cooling. Deployed in

Microsoft’s Project Natick is a different attempt to tackle this
challenge by submerging a sealed data centre under water. Tests
concluded off the Orkney Islands in 2020 showed that 864 servers
could run reliably for 2 years with cooling provided by the
ambient sea temperature, and electricity from local renewable
sources59. The potential to make use of natural cooling is
encouraging, however, the small scale of these systems could
mean higher costs, making them appropriate only for certain
high-value use cases.
ICT equipment is deployed in racks, aligned in rows, within a
data centre room. Traditional cooling manages the temperature of
the room as a whole, however, this is not as efﬁcient as more
targeted cooling. Moving from cooling the entire room to focused
cooling of a row of servers, or even a speciﬁc rack, can achieve
energy savings of up to 29%60, and is the subject of a Google
patent granted in 201261.
This is becoming necessary because of the increase in rack
density. Microsoft is deploying new hardware such as the Nvidia
DGX-2 Graphics Processing Unit that consumes 10 kW for machine
learning workloads, and existing cooling techniques are proving
insufﬁcient62. Using low-boiling-point liquids is more efﬁcient than
using ambient air cooling63 and past experiments have shown
that a super-computing system can transfer 96% of excess heat to
water64, with 45% less heat transferred to the ambient air65.
Microsoft is now testing these techniques in its cloud data
centres62.
These projects show promise for the future, but there are still
gains to be had from existing infrastructure. Google has used its AI
expertise to reduce energy use from cooling by up to 40%
through hourly adjustments to environmental controls based on
predicted weather, internal temperatures and pressure within its
existing data centres66,67. Another idea is to co-locate data centres
and desalination facilities so they can share energy intensive
operations68. That most of the innovation is now led by the big
three cloud providers demonstrates their scale advantage. By
owning, managing and controlling the entire value chain from
server design through to the location of the building, cloud
vendors have been able to push data centre efﬁciency to levels
impossible for more traditional operators to achieve.
However, only the largest providers build their own data
centres, and often work with other data centre operators in
smaller regions. For example, as of the end of 2020, Google lists 21
data centres69, publishes PUE for 1723, but has over 100 points of
presence (PoPs) around the world70. These PoPs are used to
provide services closer to its users, for example, to provide faster
load times when streaming YouTube videos71. Whilst Google owns
the equipment deployed in the PoP, it does not have the same
level of control as it does when it designs and builds its own data
centres. Even so, Google has explored efﬁciency improvements
such as optimising air venting, increasing temperature from 22 to
27 °C, deployed plastic curtains to establish cool aisles for more
heat sensitive equipment and improved the design of air
conditioning return air ﬂow. In a case study for one its PoPs, this
work was shown to reduce PUE from 2.4 to 1.7 and saved US
$67,000 per year in energy for a cost of US$25,00072.
CONCLUSIONS
Data centre water efﬁciency deserves greater attention. Annual
reports show water consumption for cooling directly paid for by
the operator, so there is an economic incentive to increase
efﬁciency. As the total energy share of cooling has fallen with
improving PUEs, the focus has been on electricity consumption,
and so water has been a low priority for the industry. However, the
largest contributor to the water footprint of a data centre is
electricity generation. Without metrics like WUEsource this is
invisible.
Moving to the cloud is more efﬁcient than running physical
infrastructure in owned or leased facilities, but transparency
remains a major issue73. Microsoft and Google both produce
detailed environmental reports, but only in aggregate. The largest
cloud provider, Amazon, publishes almost nothing at all. Facebook
is an exception, but as they do not sell cloud services, third parties
are unable to take advantage of their infrastructure in the same
way they can buy computing services from Amazon, Google or
Microsoft.
With energy consumption and carbon emissions this is starting
to change. Google and Microsoft publish their Greenhouse Gas
emissions and Microsoft has developed a Sustainability Calculator
so customers can calculate the emissions associated with their
cloud resources74. Part of the reason behind this is likely to be
pressure from customers due to legal reporting requirements now
imposed on the largest public companies75,76. However, there are
no such requirements for water.
Google and Microsoft are keen to publicise their renewable
energy projects, offset purchases, renewables matching and
energy efﬁciency improvements. Both companies publish water
consumption ﬁgures (Microsoft also includes withdrawal) but the
same level of detail provided about energy projects is lacking for
water. This is an opportunity for data centre operators to publish
more than just their PUE ratios, a metric which was never intended
to compare efﬁciency between facilities77 yet has become
standard practice to report78.
The industry has already taken the ﬁrst step by deﬁning water
metrics. Now they need to use them. Operators and cloud
vendors should calculate and publish WUEsource alongside PUE.
A breakdown of water source, such as the one published by
Digital Realty15, is also important. Using potable water diverts
valuable resources away from the local community, a situation
which is likely to get worse as water scarcity becomes more of a
problem. This would improve transparency and move the
industry from thinking mainly about use-stage energy to
considering the complete lifecycle environmental impacts of
their business.
Once metrics are introduced internally and released publicly,
data centre operators can work to improve. This starts with buying
renewable energy so that the water intensity of the energy is as
low as possible. Free cooling should be preferred but where water
is necessary for cooling, recycled and non-potable water must
make up the majority of withdrawals. Direct liquid, rack or room
cooling technologies offer greatest efﬁciency but require the ICT
equipment owner to also own, or closely work with the data
centre.
Corporate water stewardship is growing in importance79, yet it
is difﬁcult to understand the current situation due to the lack of
reporting. Google and Microsoft are leading in renewable energy,
but even they are secretive about their water resource manage-
ment. It is easy to criticise Amazon’s lack of transparency but they
are not alone—the entire data centre industry suffers from a lack
of transparency. However, they will only report data when their
customers ask for it. Organisations who lease space in data centres
must take responsibility by asking not just for PUE metrics, but
also to ask about water consumption, and make both part of their
vendor selection criteria. Considering how much data is stored in
data centres, it is ironic how little data there is available about how
they operate.
