and psychosocial stress. These effects are cumulative and long-term, 
with disproportionate impacts on rural and historically marginalized 
communities (Aerts et al., 2018; Johnson-Jennings et al., 2020).
Data centers require vast amounts of land, often converting areas 
near natural green spaces and agricultural lands into data center sites. 
Data from the Piedmont Environmental Council (2024) show that 
existing data centers in Northen Virginia currently occupy about 6,200 
acres of land, while proposed projects would add nearly 21,000 acres, 
more than tripling the current footprint in Northern Virginia alone, 
where roughly 80% of data centers are located.
Our analysis of existing and proposed data centers in Northern 
Virginia found that the 152 proposed facilities are, on average, five 
times larger than the existing 191 data centers. The rapid data center 
expansions in Northern Virginia are increasingly targeting rural land 
near national parks and agricultural land into industrial zones, posing 
risks to public health. For example, Prince William County is facing 
its largest land-use transformation in decades, with developers 
targeting 2,400 acres of undeveloped land in the Rural Crescent for 
data center construction. This area contains two federally protected 
national parks, Prince William Forest National Park and Manassas 
Battlefield National Park, which together attract over a million visitors 
annually (Regelbrugge, 2022). Moreover, over 100 additional projects 
are currently planned in Northern Virginia, collectively adding 
roughly 180 million square feet of data center space, equivalent in area 
to 1,000 Walmart Supercenters (Sierra Club, n.d.). Moreover, residents 
have raised concerns about vehicle traffic from data center 
construction, citing road damage, congestion, and blocked access for 
school buses and emergency vehicles [Joint Legislative Audit and 
Review Commission (JLARC), 2024]. This can increase local air 
pollution (e.g., particulate matter and diesel exhaust), indirectly 
contributing to respiratory and cardiovascular health risks, especially 
among vulnerable populations.
This rapid transformation threatens rural populations, 
contributing to increased psychological stress, exacerbated by limited 
healthcare access. The loss of farmland can disrupt local economies 
and erode cultural and historical ties, particularly for Indigenous 
people and farmers who see the land as central to their identity and 
psychological well-being (Johnson-Jennings et al., 2020; Reed and 
Claunch, 2020; Yazd et al., 2019; Brigance et al., 2018).
Importantly, the proximity of data centers to green spaces 
degrades ecosystems by replacing vegetation with impervious surfaces, 
fragmenting habitats, and disrupting hydrology, thus reducing their 
capacity to filter air, regulate temperature, and sustain biodiversity 
[Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission (JLARC), 2024; 
Nguyen et al., 2021]. Combined with air, water, and noise pollution 
from data centers, this ecological degradation can weaken green 
spaces’ protective functions and increase health risks in nearby 
communities. Conversely, green spaces are linked to health benefits 
by reducing air pollution and the urban heat island effect, encouraging 
physical activity, and enhancing mental health, contributing to overall 
better health and increased life expectancy (Nowak et al., 2006; Jones, 
2018; Shanahan et al., 2016). For example, increased tree cover has 
been shown to enhance natural air pollutant absorption, reducing the 
incidence of respiratory illnesses like asthma, Chronic Obstructive 
Pulmonary Disease, and cardiovascular diseases, especially among 
children (Liang et al., 2019; World Health Organization, 2016; 
Ruokolainen et al., 2015). Past research has also emphasized the 
importance of green spaces in improving the health of pregnant 
women and people with existing illnesses (Dzhambov et al., 2014; Ray 
and Jakubec, 2014). Research also emphasizes that proximity to green 
spaces is linked to better mental well-being and social support 
(Wigand et al., 2022; Aerts et al., 2018).
Economic harms and social inequality
Rising electricity demand from data centers places upward 
pressure on energy prices, indirectly affecting health through 
increased energy insecurity. Short-term impacts include heat- and 
cold-related illness due to inadequate household energy access, while 
long-term effects include chronic stress, food insecurity, and widening 
health disparities (Ballesteros-Arjona et al., 2022).
While data centers generate notable economic benefits, these 
gains are often concentrated among a select few, neglecting the 
broader public. Data centers are significant consumers of electricity, 
substantially increasing local energy demand and associated costs 
(Pipkin, 2024). According to Goldman Sachs (2024) Research, the 
data center’s global power demand is projected to grow by 160% by 
2030. In Virginia, the current energy need of data centers is estimated 
at about 5,050 MW of load and 11,000 GWh annually (Howland, 
2024). Dominion Energy anticipates that Virginia data centers will be 
the primary driver of increased energy demand over the next 15 years, 
forecasting a need for about 13.3 gigawatts by 2038 (Vogelsong, 2024). 
While these data centers currently pay the full cost of service under 
existing rate structures, their rising energy demand strains Virginia’s 
grid and could raise typical residential bills by $14–33 per month by 
2040 [Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission (JLARC), 
2024]. Wholesale electricity prices near major data center hubs have 
already increased sharply, rising by up to 267% over the past 5 years 
(Bloomberg News, 2025). These rising energy costs disproportionately 
affect lower-income households and marginalized communities, 
exacerbating existing social inequality and health disparities 
(Ballesteros-Arjona et al., 2022).
Past studies have shown that energy poverty forces vulnerable 
families to choose between paying for energy and meeting essential 
needs such as food, healthcare, and education (Pitt et al., 2022; Riva et 
al., 2023; Harrington et al., 2005). Because climate change is increasing 
the frequency of hot days, there is also a rising demand for residential 
cooling systems like air conditioning units (Colelli et al., 2023; 
Sherman et al., 2022). Rising energy costs may prevent low-income 
households from accessing adequate cooling, raising the risk of heat-
related illnesses, such as heat exhaustion and heat stroke, and 
worsening pre-existing conditions (Pitt et al., 2022; Hernández, 2013). 
Moreover, some low-income families may prioritize cooling units over 
purchasing healthy food, resulting in malnutrition and food insecurity, 
particularly among children, which can negatively affect their physical 
growth, cognitive development, and academic performance (Frank et 
al., 2006; Cook et al., 2008).
Conversely, on colder days, inadequate heating can increase 
health risks such as respiratory conditions and cardiovascular stress, 
including heart attacks and strokes (Thomson et al., 2017). Elevated 
energy costs can also contribute to poor mental health among adults, 
leading to increased anxiety, stress, and depression (Harrington et al., 
2005; Oliveras et al., 2020). Therefore, addressing the rising energy 
demands and costs associated with data centers is critical to mitigating

Potential strategies to mitigate the health 
harms of data centers
The rapid expansion of data centers, fueled by the rising demand 
for digital infrastructure, poses serious health risks that require 
coordinated mitigation across energy, water, noise, land use, 
governance and communication domains. The strategies below are 
organized by thematic risk pathways identified earlier in the paper and 
distinguish between policy-level, industry-level, and community-level 
interventions.
Energy-related strategies (policy and industry 
level)
Transitioning from fossil fuels to renewable energy for data 
centers can substantially reduce air pollution and related health issues, 
as well as lower energy costs. Ortiz et al. (2023) estimate that shifting 
to renewables for electricity production in Virginia could prevent 
deaths, reduce hospital admissions, decrease work-loss days, and save 
up to $350 million annually in health costs by 2045. Several technology 
companies have already demonstrated the feasibility of such 
transitions. For example, Microsoft’s Project Natick tested underwater 
data centers powered by offshore renewables, showing improved 
reliability and reduced environmental footprint (Roach, 2020). In 
2024, Google powered its data centers with 100% renewables and 
added 2.5 GW of clean energy, cutting emissions by 12% despite a 27% 
rise in electricity use (Google, 2024). These examples highlight the 
potential for cleaner and healthier digital infrastructure.
Water use and water quality strategies (policy and 
industry level)
Beyond cutting emissions, reducing data centers’ water 
consumption and water contamination is critical to mitigating public 
health. Using non-potable water, like Amazon’s use of recycled cooling 
water in Virginia, can ease pressure on drinking water supplies. 
Targeted cooling methods, such as shifting from whole-room to 
focused server-row cooling, can cut water use and boost energy

Noise and land-use strategies (policy and 
community level)
Further, mitigating noise pollution is essential, especially in 
residential areas near data centers. Effective strategies can include 
locating data centers away from densely populated regions and 
implementing noise reduction measures such as acoustic treatments 
and green zoning. Proactive site selection and thoughtful design, 
considering urban layout and building density, can significantly 
reduce noise-related health issues (Chan, 2023; Dzhambov and 
Dimitrova, 2014). For example, a Leesburg Virginia data center 
reduced noise pollution by re-engineering fan mounts and cutting 
low-frequency tonal noise by 20% (Compass Datacenters, 2024). 
Additionally, to limit adverse impacts from land use changes, 
policymakers should mandate responsible site selection and enforce 
zoning regulations that prioritize building data centers on existing 
industrial sites. Engaging local communities through public hearings 
and transparent decision-making processes can also help address 
residents’ concerns about environmental and health consequences.
Equity and governance strategies (policy level)
Moreover, rising energy costs associated with data center 
operations disproportionately burden low-income households. When 
demand exceeds supply, Virginia follows PJM (originally the 
Pennsylvania–New Jersey–Maryland Interconnection) curtailment 
rules prioritizing homes and critical services, but no current policy 
requires data centers to switch to backup power [Joint Legislative 
Audit and Review Commission (JLARC), 2024], increasing the risk of 
AC interruptions and related health issues during heat waves for heat-
sensitive people. Policymakers should also establish equitable energy 
pricing by introducing a dedicated data center rate class to shield 
vulnerable communities from escalating costs. Utility rates, which are 
currently adjusted every one to two years, need to be revised more 
frequently to accurately reflect cost growth [Joint Legislative Audit 
and Review Commission (JLARC), 2024]. Promoting a diversified 
energy portfolio, such as integrating renewable energy sources can 
help stabilize electricity prices and reduce dependency on fossil fuels. 
Additionally, local governments should mandate Community Benefit 
Agreements to ensure economic benefits from data centers directly 
support vulnerable populations through infrastructure enhancements, 
workforce training, and community reinvestment.
Health communication and public engagement 
strategies (policy and community level)
Finally, raising awareness about the health impacts of data centers is 
crucial for informed public and governmental decision-making. While 
community opposition to data centers, often labeled as NIMBYism (Not 
in My Backyard), frequently centers around concerns about noise, air 
and water pollution, these concerns reflect legitimate public health risks 
that demand policy attention (see Paullin, 2025; Paddison and Marsh, 
2025). Through strategic health communication, public understanding 
can be improved, and government action encouraged toward health-
focused regulation and more sustainable data center practices. 
Importantly, engaging trusted stakeholders, such as healthcare 
professionals, policymakers, and other opinion leaders, is key to this 
effort (Maibach et al., 2007; Campbell et al., 2025). Primary care doctors, 
trusted by 69% of American voters for information on global warming 
(Campbell et al., 2023), are particularly well-positioned to address public 
concerns about data centers, which raise similar health risks. Simple, 
clear, and repeated messaging from physicians and other health 
professionals can build credibility, support action-oriented advocacy, and 
help drive policy change (Maibach et al., 2014).
Limitations and possible future research 
directions
While this paper underscores the substantial health risks 
associated with data centers, it is primarily an exploratory assessment. 
As such, some limitations should be acknowledged.
First, there is the lack of data center specific epidemiological 
evidence directly linking data center operations to measured health 
outcomes. Most existing research examines related environmental 
exposures, such as air pollution, water use, noise, and heat, without 
attributing data centers as a distinct source. Second, attributing 
observed health impacts specifically to data centers is challenging in 
regions such as Northern Virginia, where multiple industrial, 
transportation, and power-generation sources coexist. Disentangling 
data center related exposures from other regional contributors 
requires high-resolution environmental monitoring and spatially 
explicit exposure assessment, which remains limited given the novelty 
of data centers as a public health research domain.
Third, this review also relies on grey literature, reflecting the 
emerging nature of the topic and the current scarcity of peer-reviewed 
studies focused explicitly on data centers and health impacts. Finally, 
this assessment is conceptual rather than quantitative and identifies 
plausible exposure pathways and health risks without estimating effect 
sizes or population-level disease burdens.
Future research should conduct quantitative, interdisciplinary 
studies that integrate physical sciences, engineering, and public health 
to directly measure emissions, exposures, and health outcomes linked 
to data center operations. Such work could assess pollutant emissions 
from increased electricity demand and their respiratory and 
cardiovascular impacts, as well as unresolved questions related to 
water demand, regional water management, noise exposure, and 
climate-related environmental and health effects. Moreover, 
expanding analyses beyond Virginia to other regions experiencing 
rapid data center growth would enable comparative assessment across 
regulatory and geographic contexts and help refine mitigation 
strategies. In addition, future studies should examine the role of 
trusted opinion leaders such as healthcare professionals, policymakers, 
and government officials and effective communication strategies, 
including message framing, to enhance issue awareness and positively 
influence public attitudes and behaviors.

Conclusion
As data centers expand, both existing and proposed facilities pose 
significant health and environmental challenges that demand urgent 
action. Policymakers must mitigate harms from operational data 
centers by enforcing stricter environmental regulations, monitoring 
emissions, and mandating mitigation measures to protect surrounding 
communities. Transparency is essential. Residents have the right to 
know the risks associated with data centers and should be actively 
informed about industry practices. Conversely, developers must engage 
the public to address their concerns, especially as opposition grows 
under NIMBY movements. Moreover, for proposed new data centers, 
public input must guide decision-making—do residents want them, 
and if so, under what conditions? Developers must adhere to clear 
design and operational safeguards, including renewable energy 
integration, water conservation, noise pollution control measures, and 
responsible land siting. By prioritizing sustainability, data centers can 
achieve responsible growth without compromising public health.

National Laboratory of the Rockies    |    3
Water Planning with Context
Water planning needs a defined system, source, and stress period.
SYSTEM BOUNDARY
What is included?
Full campus and phases, every source and backup, evaporation, discharge, lost 
return flow, sewer service and water used to generate electricity. Public supply 
does not remove watershed impacts. [1, 3]
PLACE AND SOURCE
Where does the effect land?
Utility source mix, watershed or aquifer, connected streams, basin transfers, 
water quality, water rights and available infrastructure capacity. Reclaimed 
water can still reduce downstream return flows. [3, 9]
TIME AND STRESS
When is supply constrained?
Monthly and peak-day or peak-hour demand during heat, drought, low flow, 
outages and startup, from current use to full buildout. Potomac summer monthly 
use can approach 3 times average and peak daily use 10 times average. [3]
[1] Shehabi and colleagues (2024), section 5. [3] Interstate Commission on the Potomac River Basin (2026).
[9] Barlow and Leake (2012), Streamflow Depletion by Wells, United States Geological Survey Circular 1376.
Full linked references and the basis for the planning framework are in speaker notes.

National Laboratory of the Rockies    |    4
Water Impacts and Decision Context
Water planning also needs impact definitions and affected-use context.
QUANTITY AND QUALITY
What kind of water impact?
Separate withdrawal (water used), consumption 
(water that leaves the system), discharge and 
storage. Track drinking-quality and reclaimed water, 
return-flow timing, heat, salts, chemicals and 
concentrated waste. [3, 4, 7]
AFFECTED USES AND
CUMULATIVE EFFECTS
Who or what bears the risk?
Public supply and customer cost, downstream users, 
fish and habitat, Tribal rights and cultural uses, 
nearby projects and climate stress. Tribal authority 
and rights vary by place. [3, 5, 6]
WATER METRICS NEED CONTEXT
State how demand and availability are defined, how environmental flows and managed supplies are treated, the 
spatial and temporal resolution, threshold rationale, data year and uncertainty. [8]
DECISION IMPLICATION: Use source-specific water balances, stress cases, discharge and return-flow effects, 
fisheries and cultural-use screening, electricity-related water, cumulative impacts and measured performance. [1, 3–8]
[4] United States Geological Survey (2019). [5] Virginia Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission (2024).
[6] National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Fisheries. [7] Environmental Protection Agency, Quincy case study.
[8] Kuzma and colleagues (2023), Aqueduct 4.0.

metadata.name: Istidamah al-Mawarid al-Tabi’iyyah in Artificial Intelligence Era: Study on Water Resource Governance for Data Centers

GD90.full_text:
Istidamah al-Mawarid al-Tabi'iyyah in Artificial 
Intelligence Era: Study on Water Resource Governance 
for Data Centers 
Agung Tri Wicaksono 1
 and Sri Warjiyati 2
1,2  Universitas Islam Negeri Sunan Ampel, Surabaya 60237, Indonesia 
agungren1745@gmail.com 
Abstract. Data center water consumption grows in step with artificial 
intelligence workloads, and the Annual and Sustainability Report published by 
PT DCI Indonesia for fiscal year 2025 shows this pattern at facility scale in 
Indonesia. This study asks whether Islamic legal doctrine can supply a normative 
ceiling that secular efficiency-based regulation currently lacks. This is a 
normative-juridical study using statutory, comparative, and conceptual 
approaches. Comparative analysis covers the water governance regimes of 
Singapore, the Netherlands, and the United States. Conceptual analysis draws on 
istidamah al-mawarid al-tabi'iyyah, maqasid al-syari'ah (hifz al-nafs), la darar wa 
la dirar, and mizan. All quantitative data are drawn from PT DCI Indonesia's 
Annual and Sustainability Report 2025; a 2026 projection for the E2 Surabaya 
facility is calculated from the company's own disclosed water-to-electricity ratio. 
Disclosed water usage across DCI's facilities rose 161% between 2023 and 2025, 
from 233,586 m³ to 610,833 m³. Applying DCI's 2025 water-to-electricity ratio 
to E2 Surabaya's 9 MW installed capacity projects approximately 134,700 m³ of 
water consumption for April-December 2026 under a full-load scenario. None of 
the three secular regimes examined impose an absolute consumption ceiling 
comparable to what la darar wa la dirar would require, pointing toward a hybrid 
governance model combining an absolute threshold, waqf-linked conservation 
financing, and mandatory pre-approval harm assessment. 
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Data Center; Islamic Environmental Law; 
Istidamah Al-Mawarid Al-Tabi'iyyah; Water Governance. 
1 
Introduction 
 
 
© The Author(s) 2026 
U. Faruq et al. (eds.), Proceedings of the 10th International Conference of Islamic Studies (ICONIS 2026) & 
400th Anniversary of Shekh Yusuf Al-Makassari, Advances in Social Science, Education and Humanities 
Research 1043, 
https://doi.org/10.2991/978-94-6239-845-0_15
PT DCI Indonesia's Annual and Sustainability Report 2025 records water usage rising 
from 233,586 m³ in 2023 to 376,116 m³ in 2024, then to 610,833 m³ in 2025, a 161% 
increase across two years [1]. Electricity usage over the same period rose from 
127,572,458 kWh to 264,030,977 kWh, a 107% increase. Water consumption outpaced 
electricity consumption, a pattern that runs against the usual assumption that cooling 
efficiency upgrades should slow water demand relative to computing load. These 
figurecome from a single facility operator in Surabaya, but they sit inside a much larger 
global trend that has developed largely without a corresponding governance response. 

 
Artificial intelligence workloads require sustained, high-density computation, and 
high-density computation generates heat that most data centers remove through water-
based cooling [2].  Training and running large AI models at scale has turned water, 
alongside electricity, into one of the two resource inputs that determine whether a data 
center can keep operating during periods of drought or grid stress. Large technology 
companies have begun disclosing consumption figures at a scale that makes the 
underlying pressure visible: Google reported 6.4 billion gallons of water used across its 
data centers in 2023, and Microsoft reported 2 billion gallons in the same year [3].  Both 
figures came from voluntary corporate sustainability reporting, not from compliance 
against any binding withdrawal ceiling, because no such ceiling currently applies to 
either company at the scale these numbers represent.  
Indonesia's domestic data center sector is following a comparable trajectory, at an 
earlier stage but at a steep growth rate. Market research projects the domestic data 
center water consumption market to grow at a compound annual rate of approximately 
18%, reaching an estimated 37.80 billion liters in 2025 [4].  E2 Data Center Surabaya, 
one of PT DCI Indonesia's facilities, carries 9 MW of total IT load and sits adjacent to 
Surabaya's main internet exchange at Intiland Tower, offering direct connectivity to 
major cloud providers. The 2025 Annual and Sustainability Report does not 
disaggregate water usage by individual facility within DCI's portfolio, so no directly 
reported figure yet exists for E2 Surabaya specifically. This study addresses that gap 
using a calculation, not an assumption, applying DCI's own 2025 company-wide water-
to-electricity ratio to E2 Surabaya's 9 MW capacity under a full-load scenario for April 
to December 2026. Table 1 sets out this calculation step by step. 
Table 1. Projection Method for E2 Surabaya Water Consumption, April to December 2026.

224             A. T. Wicaksono and S. Warjiyati

 
 
 
This calculation uses no figure external to DCI's own 2025 disclosure and the 
publicly stated IT load capacity of E2 Surabaya. It assumes full-load operation 
throughout the projection window, which represents an upper-bound scenario rather 
than an average-case estimate; actual 2026 consumption may fall below this figure if 
the facility operates below full load during its initial months. 
Fig. 1. PT DCI Indonesia Water and Electricity Usage, 2023 to 2025, with E2 Surabaya 2026 
Projection 
Two bodies of scholarship address the underlying problem from separate directions, 
and neither, on its own, accounts for the pattern visible in DCI's disclosed numbers [1]. 
One body of work is regulatory and comparative. It documents Singapore's 2019 
moratorium on new data center approvals as a case of an absolute administrative ceiling 
[5], the Netherlands' practice of negotiating water-use agreements directly between 
regional water authorities and hyperscale operators as a case of accommodation 
handled agreement by agreement, and the United States' devolved, state-level drought 
contingency planning as a case of localized deference with no unifying federal standard 
[6]. Within this literature, a live debate concerns whether efficiency metrics such as 
Water Usage Effectiveness are sufficient on their own to manage rising data center 
water demand, or whether some form of absolute limit is eventually unavoidable [7].  
The second body of work is doctrinal rather than regulatory. Scholarship on fiqh al-
bi'ah (Islamic environmental jurisprudence) has developed water and natural resources 
as objects of ecological trusteeship, grounding this trusteeship in maqasid al-syari'ah 
and operationalizing it through maxims such as la darar wa la dirar. This literature has 
rarely been tested against a specific, contemporary infrastructure case, and almost never 
against the particular water-intensity profile of artificial intelligence data centers, where 
consumption growth is driven by computing scale rather than by conventional industrial 
output. The result is a conceptual gap between two mature but separate literatures: one 
measures efficiency without asking whether efficiency is the right unit of concern, and 
Istidamah al-Mawarid al-Tabi’iyyah in Artificial Intelligence …             225

 
the other articulates trusteeship without yet applying it to the infrastructure generating 
the fastest-growing water demand of the current decade. 
DCI's own disclosed numbers illustrate why closing this gap carries practical weight, 
not just theoretical interest. A facility can adopt a genuinely more efficient cooling 
technology, as DCI states it has done through its chilled-water system, and still register 
a 161% increase in absolute water consumption over two years. Efficiency ratios 
measure water used per unit of computation; they do not measure, and are not designed 
to measure, total volume withdrawn from a shared watershed. When the scale of 
computing demand grows faster than the efficiency gains applied to it, an efficiency-
compliant facility and a rapidly water-depleting facility can be the same facility, 
reported through the same set of metrics, in the same year. 
Islamic legal doctrine approaches this same water through a different set of 
questions. Rather than asking how much water was used per unit of output, istidamah 
al-mawarid al-tabi'iyyah asks whether water has been held as amanah (a trust) on 
behalf of a community and of future users who depend on the same watershed. Maqasid 
al-syari'ah, through the specific objective of hifz al-nafs (preservation of life), treats 
water access as directly bound to the preservation of life rather than as an externality to 
be priced into an efficiency calculation. The maxim la darar wa la dirar shifts the 
burden of proof: instead of permitting withdrawal until harm is demonstrated after the 
fact, it requires an operator to show, before approval, that no harm will result. Mizan 
frames the entire arrangement as a balance to be maintained among the operator's 
commercial interest, the community's subsistence need, and the watershed's capacity to 
recover, rather than as a negotiation between two parties or a limit imposed from a 
single administrative center. 
This study places these doctrinal principles against the same set of numbers used to 
describe DCI E2 Surabaya's water consumption, rather than treating the two as separate 
exercises running in parallel. Reading a 161% two-year consumption increase through 
the lens of la darar wa la dirar produces a different research question than reading the 
same number through a Water Usage Effectiveness ratio: the doctrinal question asks 
whether harm has occurred, or is likely to occur, to other water users, independent of 
whatever efficiency claim accompanies the increase. That distinction, between 
measuring efficiency and assessing harm, organizes the remainder of this study. 
Three research questions follow. First, how do the water governance regimes of 
Singapore, the Netherlands, and the United States respond to industrial and data center 
water demand, and at what point does each regime stop short of imposing an absolute 
consumption ceiling (RQ1)? Second, what does Islamic legal doctrine, namely 
istidamah al-mawarid al-tabi'iyyah, maqasid al-syari'ah, la darar wa la dirar, and 
mizan, contribute to this analysis that efficiency-based secular regulation does not 
already provide (RQ2)? Third, what hybrid governance model follows from combining 
these doctrinal principles with the regulatory instruments examined under RQ1, and 
how does the disclosed and projected DCI and E2 Surabaya data test the practical shape 
of that model (RQ3)? 
226             A. T. Wicaksono and S. Warjiyati

 
 
 
2 
Method 
This study uses normative-juridical legal research, conducted through the analysis of 
legal materials and documentary sources rather than through field observation, 
interviews, or survey instruments [8].  The research question concerns the interpretation 
of legal doctrine and its integration with comparative regulatory frameworks, which 
places the inquiry within the domain of doctrinal legal analysis rather than empirical 
social research [9]. No primary field data collection was undertaken for this study, and 
every quantitative figure discussed in the Result and Discussion section traces back to 
a single published corporate document, PT DCI Indonesia's Annual and Sustainability 
Report 2025, a limitation stated explicitly rather than obscured. 
Three analytical approaches structure the research, applied to three tiers of legal 
materials [10]. The statutory approach is applied to primary legal materials consisting 
of the regulatory instruments of Singapore's Public Utilities Board, including the 2019 
moratorium on new data center approvals; Dutch regional water authority frameworks 
governing negotiated water-use agreements; United States state-level drought 
contingency planning statutes; and the Qur'an and Hadith as primary sources of Islamic 
law. The comparative approach places these three regulatory regimes alongside one 
another and against the doctrinal framework developed from Islamic legal sources,  in 
order to identify where secular regulatory instruments converge with, or diverge from, 
the precautionary logic embedded in la darar wa la dirar. The conceptual approach 
(pendekatan konseptual) is applied to secondary legal materials, consisting of fiqh al-
bi'ah scholarship, contemporary Islamic finance literature on waqf-based conservation 
financing, and academic journal articles analyzing the three regulatory regimes, 
together with tertiary materials such as legal dictionaries used to clarify technical and 
doctrinal terminology where needed [11].  
Data collection follows standard library research technique: the primary, secondary, 
and tertiary legal materials described above were identified, read, and organized 
according to the three analytical approaches [12],  then cross-referenced against the 
empirical and projected figures already presented in Table 1 of the Introduction. 
Analysis proceeds through qualitative-deductive legal reasoning, in which the 
regulatory logic identified under the statutory approach is compared against the 
doctrinal principles identified under the conceptual approach, and both are read against 
the disclosed and projected DCI and E2 Surabaya figures, in order to construct the 
hybrid governance model that answers RQ3 in the Result and Discussion section. 
3 
Result and Discussion 
Three sets of findings answer the three research questions posed in the Introduction. 
The first set compares how Singapore, the Netherlands, and the United States regulate 
industrial and data center water demand, read against the full water and electricity 
dataset disclosed in PT DCI Indonesia's Annual and Sustainability Report 2025. The 
second set applies the four Islamic legal principles introduced earlier to the same 
dataset, asking what those principles reveal that a Water Usage Effectiveness ratio does 
Istidamah al-Mawarid al-Tabi’iyyah in Artificial Intelligence …             227

 
 
not. The third set combines both lines of analysis into a hybrid governance model, tested 
against DCI's position as Indonesia's largest integrated data center operator. 
3.1 
Secular Water Governance Regimes and the DCI Dataset 
Table 2 reproduces the full environmental disclosure from PT DCI Indonesia's Annual 
and Sustainability Report 2025, extending the water and electricity figures already 
introduced in the Introduction with the report's hazardous waste data. 
Table 2. Environmental Aspect Disclosure, PT DCI Indonesia, 2023 to

Source: PT DCI Indonesia, Annual and Sustainability Report 2025. 
Water usage climbed 61% from 2023 to 2024 and a further 62% from 2024 to 2025, 
compounding to the 161% two-year increase noted earlier [1]. Electricity usage climbed 
at a slower compound rate of 107% across the same period. Hazardous waste output 
moved in neither direction consistently, falling to 0.175 tons in 2024 before rising to 
56.92 tons in 2025, a pattern the report does not explain and that this study does not 
attempt to interpret beyond noting its irregularity relative to the steadier water and 
electricity trends. 
The report also breaks water usage down by type, distinguishing industrial 
withdrawal from wastewater output. Table 3 reproduces this breakdown. 
Table 3. Water Usage by Type, PT DCI Indonesia, 2023 to 2025 
Type of Water

Source: PT DCI Indonesia, Annual and Sustainability Report 2025. 
Total water flow through the facility, industrial withdrawal combined with 
wastewater output, rose from 349,131 m³ in 2023 to 840,506 m³ in 2025, a 141% 
increase [13]. Wastewater itself grew more slowly than industrial withdrawal, rising 
99% across the same period compared to the 161% rise in industrial water.  Read as a 
ratio, wastewater fell from 49.5% of industrial withdrawal in 2023 to 37.6% in 2025, 
meaning a growing share of the water drawn into the facility did not return as 
measurable wastewater output. Evaporative loss through cooling operations is one 
plausible explanation for this gap, consistent with the report's own description of a 
chilled-water cooling system, though the report does not itself quantify evaporative loss 
as a separate category. 
These figures describe PT DCI Indonesia at the company level, not E2 Surabaya 
alone, and the scale of the company matters to how the E2 Surabaya figures should be 
read. Industry mapping of Indonesia's data center sector places PT DCI Indonesia Tbk 
228             A. T. Wicaksono and S. Warjiyati

 
 
 
as the largest integrated data center provider in the country, with total capacity 
exceeding 100 MW spread across multiple locations, and with public company status 
following its listing. E2 Surabaya's 9 MW of installed IT load represents roughly 9% 
of that total portfolio capacity, meaning the company-wide water figures in Tables 2 
and 3 already reflect consumption across a footprint several times larger than the single 
facility this study projects for 2026. 
Read against that scale, the 134,700 m³ projection calculated in Table 1 describes 
only one node in a larger network, not the full extent of DCI's operations. If comparable 
facilities elsewhere in DCI's portfolio operate at similar water intensity per megawatt, 
the company-wide trend documented in Table 2 gives a more accurate sense of 
aggregate exposure than any single-facility projection can. This matters for how RQ1 
should be answered: a regulatory regime built around facility-by-facility review, as both 
the Dutch and American models effectively are, may systematically understate the 
water demand of an operator whose footprint spans a dozen or more sites [14].  
Singapore's approach avoids that particular blind spot by regulating at the level of 
new approvals rather than individual facility performance. The 2019 moratorium on 
new data center approvals stopped additional capacity from entering the market 
altogether, rather than asking each new facility to justify its water use against an 
efficiency benchmark [15]. This is an administrative ceiling applied before 
construction, not a performance standard applied after operation begins, and it sidesteps 
the aggregation problem identified above because it constrains total sector capacity 
directly rather than summing facility-level compliance reports. 
The Netherlands takes the opposite structural position. Regional water authorities 
negotiate withdrawal volumes with hyperscale operators on a case-by-case basis,  an 
approach that gives each negotiation room to account for local watershed conditions 
but that also means no single agreement captures the cumulative demand of an operator 
with facilities spread across multiple water authority jurisdictions [16]. A company with 
the multi-site footprint described in the industry mapping above could, under this 
model, negotiate separately with each relevant regional authority without any single 
authority holding a complete picture of the company's aggregate water demand. 
The United States compounds this fragmentation further by devolving water 
governance to individual states, each running its own drought contingency planning 
process with no federal coordination tying the states together [17].  Commentary within 
this literature increasingly debates whether efficiency improvements alone can resolve 
the resulting water pressure, without resort to any binding cap.7 The DCI dataset offers 
a partial answer to that debate: efficiency investment, in the form of the chilled-water 
system described in the sustainability report, coincided with a 161% increase in 
industrial water withdrawal, not a decline in it. 
Indonesia's current regulatory position resembles the American model in its lack of 
a unifying national ceiling, but without the state-level drought contingency 
infrastructure that at least gives the American system some minimum planning 
architecture. Given that PT DCI Indonesia alone accounts for more than 100 MW of 
installed capacity across multiple sites, a regulatory gap at the national level does not 
describe a marginal case; it describes the water governance framework applicable to 
Istidamah al-Mawarid al-Tabi’iyyah in Artificial Intelligence …             229

 
 
 
the country's largest data center operator, and by extension to a large share of the 
sector's aggregate water demand [18]. 
Figure 2 sets out these four regulatory postures side by side, positioned along a 
spectrum from absolute restriction to full deference, with Indonesia's current position 
marked as unresolved. 
 
Fig. 2. Regulatory Spectrum: Absolute Ceiling to Undefined 
Table 4 summarizes the comparative regulatory logic discussed above, isolating the 
specific dimension each regime leaves unaddressed.

230             A. T. Wicaksono and S. Warjiyati

 
 
 
None of the three established regimes examined here resolves the aggregation 
problem identified in the DCI dataset: an operator's water footprint measured at the 
level of an individual facility, or even at the level of a single negotiated agreement, can 
understate the operator's total demand once its full multi-site portfolio is taken into 
account. This gap is the starting point for the doctrinal analysis that follows. 
3.2 
Islamic Doctrinal Contribution Applied to the DCI Dataset 
The four principles introduced in the Introduction, istidamah al-mawarid al-
tabi'iyyah, maqasid al-syari'ah, la darar wa la dirar, and mizan, address the gaps 
identified in Table 4 by asking a different question than any of the three secular 
regimes ask. Where Singapore asks whether new capacity should be approved at 
all, the Netherlands asks what volume a specific facility may withdraw, and the 
United States asks whether a given state's drought plan has been followed, 
istidamah al-mawarid al-tabi'iyyah asks whether the water drawn by any of these 
arrangements has been treated as amanah, a trust held on behalf of the 
watershed's other users, independent of which regulatory instrument happens to 
apply [19]. 
Applied to the DCI dataset, this principle does not treat the 161% rise in industrial 
water withdrawal as a number to be judged efficient or inefficient. It treats the number 
as a claim on a shared resource that must be justified against the interests of everyone 
else who depends on the same watershed, a justification that neither the moratorium 
model, the negotiated model, nor the devolved model requires as a matter of course. 
The 100 MW multi-site footprint documented earlier makes this justification harder to 
satisfy at the level of a single company than it would be for a smaller operator, precisely 
because the trust obligation compounds across every site the company operates, not just 
the one under review. 
Hifz al-nafs, the preservation of life objective within maqasid al-syari'ah, gives this 
trust obligation a specific point of reference: the water access of communities living 
near each facility [20].  DCI's own disclosure states that water treatment is handled by 
the surrounding industrial estate, which means the company's water relationship runs 
through an intermediary rather than directly through a municipal or community water 
authority. From a hifz al-nafs standpoint, this intermediary arrangement does not 
resolve the question of community water access; it relocates the question to the 
industrial estate's own water allocation decisions, a layer of the supply chain that the 
sustainability report does not describe and that this study's normative-juridical method, 
relying on the report alone, cannot examine further [21].  
La darar wa la dirar addresses this same gap by placing the burden of proof on the 
party best positioned to demonstrate the absence of harm before withdrawal begins, 
rather than after [22].  None of the three secular regimes in Table 4 apply this sequencing 
consistently: Singapore's moratorium restricts new entry but does not require a harm 
assessment from facilities approved before 2019; the Dutch model negotiates volume 
but does not require the operator to prove the absence of harm as a precondition of 
negotiation; the American model reviews compliance against a drought plan that, being 
state specific, cannot account for harm accruing across state lines. A rule built on la 
Istidamah al-Mawarid al-Tabi’iyyah in Artificial Intelligence …             231

 
darar wa la dirar would require PT DCI Indonesia to demonstrate, before any expansion 
at E2 Surabaya or at any other site, that the community and ecosystem served by the 
same watershed will not be harmed by the additional withdrawal implied by the Table 
1 projection. 
Mizan supplies the frame that holds the other three principles together at the scale 
relevant to an operator the size of PT DCI Indonesia. Balance, in this context, is not a 
balance struck once between one operator and one regulator, as the Dutch model 
implies, but a balance maintained across every site an operator controls, weighed 
against every community and watershed those sites draw from. A company with over 
100 MW of capacity spread across multiple locations tests this principle more severely 
than a single small facility would, because the mizan obligation does not shrink simply 
because the demand is distributed across several sites rather than concentrated in one 
[23].  
Table 5 maps each doctrinal principle against the specific regulatory gap it addresses, 
drawing directly on the comparative analysis in Table 4. 
Table 5. Doctrinal Principles Mapped Against Secular Regulatory

Figure 3 illustrates how these four principles relate to one another and to the water 
governance outcome they jointly inform, with mizan positioned as the organizing frame 
around the other three. 
232             A. T. Wicaksono and S. Warjiyati

 
 
 
 
Fig. 3. Doctrinal Framework: Mizan as Organizing Principle. 
Read together, the four principles in Table 5 and Figure 3 do not add a fifth regulatory 
instrument alongside the three already examined under RQ1. They change the default 
assumption each instrument operates from. Singapore's moratorium restricts entry by 
default; the Dutch and American models permit withdrawal by default, subject to 
negotiation or state level review. A regime built on la darar wa la dirar permits 
withdrawal only once harm has been ruled out [24], a default distinct from all three 
secular models and one that carries particular weight for an operator whose aggregate 
footprint, as documented in Table 4, already exceeds what any single facility level 
review is designed to capture. 
3.3 
A Hybrid Governance Model Tested Against the DCI Dataset 
The gaps identified in Table 4 and the doctrinal responses mapped in Table 5 point 
toward three governance components, each addressing a specific limitation rather than 
replacing the secular instruments already in place. The first component is an absolute 
consumption threshold, following the logic of Singapore's 2019 moratorium but applied 
at the level of aggregate company capacity rather than only at the point of new facility 
approval [25].  Calibrated this way, the threshold would apply to PT DCI Indonesia's 
full multi-site footprint, not solely to E2 Surabaya, closing the aggregation gap 
identified in Table 4 without requiring Singapore's more restrictive step of halting new 
approvals altogether. 
The second component is a waqf-linked conservation financing mechanism,[26] 
under which an operator's contribution scales with its aggregate footprint rather than 
with any single facility's disclosed figures. For a company the size of PT DCI Indonesia, 
with capacity exceeding 100 MW across multiple sites, this contribution would 
necessarily exceed what a single-facility calculation such as the Table 1 projection 
would suggest, because the financing obligation under istidamah al-mawarid al-
Istidamah al-Mawarid al-Tabi’iyyah in Artificial Intelligence …             233

 
 
tabi'iyyah attaches to the trust relationship the company holds across its entire portfolio, 
not to any one site in isolation. 
The third component is a mandatory harm-impact assessment required before 
approval, built directly on la darar wa la dirar, and applied cumulatively across an 
operator's full site portfolio rather than facility by facility. Under current practice, as 
documented in Table 4, review happens after the fact and at the level of an individual 
facility or agreement. A cumulative pre-approval requirement would instead ask PT 
DCI Indonesia to demonstrate, before any further expansion, that its aggregate 
withdrawal across all sites, projected using the same method applied to E2 Surabaya in 
Table 1, will not compromise water access for communities served by the same 
watersheds. 
Table 6 summarizes these three components against the regulatory gap and doctrinal 
principle each one answers.

Two risks qualify this model, and both become more visible once the analysis is 
scaled to an operator the size of PT DCI Indonesia rather than to a single facility. The 
first risk concerns the institutional capacity of waqf bodies to manage financing 
obligations calculated against a multi-site, over 100 MW portfolio, a scale considerably 
larger than most existing Indonesian waqf institutions have managed to date. The 
second risk is jurisdictional arbitrage, and the multi-site structure documented in this 
study's data makes this risk concrete rather than hypothetical: an operator already 
spanning multiple locations within Indonesia could concentrate future expansion in 
provinces with weaker enforcement of the proposed threshold, without needing to cross 
a national border to do so, unlike the Johor or Arizona cases discussed in comparative 
literature on cross-border arbitrage [27]. 
234             A. T. Wicaksono and S. Warjiyati

 
 
 
Figure 4 sets out the sequencing of the three components as a licensing pathway, 
positioned against the aggregate portfolio scale relevant to an operator such as PT DCI 
Indonesia. 
 
Fig. 4. Hybrid Governance Model: Sequential Licensing Pathway 
Tested against PT DCI Indonesia's disclosed figures, this hybrid model does not ask 
whether E2 Surabaya's projected 134,700 m³ for 2026 is efficient. It asks whether that 
figure, added to whatever comparable demand exists across the rest of the company's 
over 100 MW portfolio, has been justified in advance against the interests of the 
communities and watersheds the full portfolio touches. That reframing, from a single 
facility's efficiency ratio to a company's aggregate trust obligation, is this study's answer 
to RQ3, and it depends on reading the doctrinal principles developed under RQ2 
directly against the scale of operation documented under RQ1. 
4 
Conclusion 
Three regulatory postures, an absolute ceiling in Singapore, a negotiated 
accommodation in the Netherlands, and a devolved deference in the United States, each 
leave a different dimension of data center water demand unaddressed, and none of the 
three is built to capture the aggregate footprint of an operator whose capacity spans 
multiple sites, as PT DCI Indonesia's own disclosure demonstrates. The most notable 
finding here is not that DCI's water consumption grew, but that it grew fastest in the 
same period the company invested in more efficient cooling technology: the chilled-
water system described in the 2025 sustainability report accompanied a 161% increase 
in industrial water withdrawal between 2023 and 2025, rather than a slowdown in it. 
Efficiency and absolute consumption moved in the same direction, not opposite ones, 
which suggests that a regulatory model built solely on efficiency reporting would have 
approved this trend rather than questioned it. Islamic legal doctrine responds to this 
finding by asking a question none of the three secular regimes ask as a matter of course, 
namely whether the water drawn by an operator's full portfolio, not just one facility, 
Istidamah al-Mawarid al-Tabi’iyyah in Artificial Intelligence …             235

 
 
has been treated as amanah owed to the surrounding watershed and its other users. Read 
through istidamah al-mawarid al-tabi'iyyah, hifz al-nafs, la darar wa la dirar, and mizan, 
the hybrid model proposed in this study, an absolute consumption threshold calibrated 
to company-wide capacity, a waqf-linked conservation financing obligation scaled to 
that same footprint, and a mandatory pre-approval harm assessment applied 
cumulatively, offers a governance architecture that neither the Singaporean, Dutch, nor 
American models currently provide on their own. This model, and the doctrinal 
reasoning that produced it, is this study's central contribution. 
This study is limited by its reliance on a single published source, PT DCI Indonesia's 
Annual and Sustainability Report 2025, for every quantitative figure discussed, a 
constraint that follows directly from the normative-juridical method chosen rather than 
from any attempt to set aside the value of field verification. The projected 134,700 m³ 
figure for E2 Surabaya remains an upper-bound estimate calculated from the company's 
own reported ratios rather than a measured outcome, and the more than 100 MW multi-
site capacity figure used to frame the aggregation problem in the Result and Discussion 
section comes from industry mapping rather than from DCI's own audited disclosure, a 
gap that independent verification would still need to close. Future research should test 
the hybrid governance model proposed here against other Indonesian data center 
operators identified in the same industry mapping, extend the comparative regulatory 
analysis beyond the three jurisdictions examined in this study, and, where field access 
becomes available, verify the aggregate multi-site water figures that this study was only 
able to estimate from public disclosure.

Analyzing Data Centers' Impacts on the Environment and Pathways to 
Sustainability 
 
 
Manisha Bharambe1, Poonam Ponde2, Harshita Vachhani3, Smita Ghorpade4, Dipita Dhande5 
 
Submitted: 05/11/2024          Revised: 12/12/2024          Accepted: 26/12/2024 
Abstract: In the digital era, due to huge data generation across various sectors, there is a need to store and process a vast amount of data. 
Data centers play a crucial role in this demand to support everything from internet services to cloud computing and manage a huge 
amount of information. As demand rises globally, the need for data centers increases. However, Data centers have serious environmental 
consequences associated with their quick growth. Due to their ongoing operation and cooling requirements, data centers are energy-
intensive, which raises carbon emissions and the need for electricity. The strain on the environment and natural resources increases with 
the size of the global digital footprint. Data centers have a significant environmental impact due to their high electricity consumption, 
substantial water usage, and the materials used in their construction. This research paper aims to investigate the ecological impacts of 
data centers, focusing on electricity consumption, carbon emissions, and resource utilization. This research focuses on analyzing the 
impact of data centers and finding the pathways to mitigate it. The tree plantation near to data centers and the geographical area should 
be consider while building the data centers. 
 
Keywords: Data centers, Environment, digital footprint, electricity consumption, digital footprint, Tree plantation, carbon emission 
 
1. Introduction 
 
Environmentalists, regulators, and business stakeholders are all 
worried about data centers. Data centers can employ immersion 
cooling systems and more efficient energy systems to lessen their 
environmental impact. Additionally, they have the option of 
using recycled or reclaimed water in place of freshwater.  
Renewable Energy: To lessen their carbon footprint, many data 
centers 
are switching to 
renewable 
energy 
sources like solar and wind power. The data centers of large 
corporations such as Google, Amazon, and Microsoft are now 
powered entirely by renewable energy.  
Energy 
Efficiency: Improvements in 
cooling 
technologies 
(like liquid cooling and free-air cooling) and server optimization 
help lower the energy needed to operate data centers.  
Green Data Centers: To lessen their environmental effect, some 
designs and employing 
businesses are implementing energy-
efficient environmentally friendly technologies, such as using 
recycled water for cooling or situating data centers in colder 
regions to lower cooling requirements.                     
 
The backbone 
of contemporary digital 
infrastructure, data 
centers are crucial for processing, storing, and sharing massive 
volumes of data. Because of their massive energy use and 
dependence on 
non-renewable 
energy resources, 
their 
environmental 
impact 
has 
become 
a 
rising 
worry. Continuous operation of backup power, cooling systems, 
and servers consumes natural resources and produces massive 
carbon 
dioxide 
emissions. Understanding the 
environmental 
impact of data centers and investigating sustainable solutions 
is essential to 
reducing 
their 
ecological 
footprint 
and addressing climate change as digital demands increase 
worldwide. 
 
Environmental impact Factors: 
High energy requirements: To run servers, networks, and 
cooling equipment, data centers use a lot of electricity. It is 
thought that between 1-2% of the world's electricity is used by 
data centers worldwide, and this figure is even greater in certain 
areas. In 2023, U.S. data centers contributed over 105 million 
tons of CO2e emissions, representing 2.18% of total U.S. 
emissions. 
Water consumption: Data centers use a lot of water to keep their 
servers and other equipment cool. This water can come from 
potable water sources, which can be a valuable resource for local 
communities. The data centers have an average Water Use 
Efficiency 
(WUE) of 1.9 
liters 
per 
kilowatt-hour(kWh). 
Water Wastage: Even 
in 
regions 
with 
plenty 
of water, 
the overuse of water for cooling can still be harmful and have

Carbon Footprint: The energy source is crucial. The majority 
of data centers rely on fossil fuels to generate electricity, which 
releases large amounts of carbon dioxide (CO2). Data centers are 
a part of the IT industry, which might account for up to 3.7% 
of all GHG emissions worldwide.  
Increasing Demand: The energy needs of data centers are rising 
along with the expansion of big data, cloud services, streaming, 
and AI apps, which is making their environmental effect worse. 
Data centers in the United States used around 17 gigawatts (GW) 
of electricity in 
2022, which 
rise to 
176 terawatt 
hours in 
2023, accounting for 4.4% of the country's total electricity 
consumption. 
Destruction of natural habitat: Data centers require large areas 
of 
land 
to 
be 
cleared 
for 
construction. 
Waste and disposal: The large amount of e-waste generated by 
data centers may include dangerous substances like lead and 
mercury, cadmium and other toxic chemicals. These materials 
can pollute the soil and water if they are not properly disposed of. 
E-waste (electronic waste): The lifespan of the equipment is 
short: Due to upgrades and performance needs, the hardware in 
data centers, like servers and storage equipment, is frequently 
replaced every few 
years. As a result, 
there 
is 
a 
significant amount of e-waste, some of which contains hazardous 
chemicals like lead, mercury, and cadmium that can harmful for 
the environment, so they should recycled appropriately. 
Obstacles to Recycling: Due to the intricacy of the materials, it 
is challenging to recycle many pieces of data center equipment, 
resulting 
in landfill buildup. 
Production: The production 
of data 
center 
hardware, such 
as servers, routers, and cables, can result in pollution and habitat 
loss. 
 
OBJECTIVE 
I. 
 Energy Consumption measure: To quantify the 
energy demands of data centers and their contribution 
to global electricity consumption and greenhouse gas 
emissions. 
II. 
Evaluation of Sustainable Practices: To explore 
advanced cooling technologies, energy-efficient 
architectures, and the integration of renewable 
energy sources as methods to mitigate environmental 
impacts. 
 
2. 
LITERATURE REVIEW 
 
Daniel Ewim et al.(2018) [1]:The solution to the environmental 
challenges posed by data centres lies in improving energy 
efficiency and adopting sustainable practices. Key strategies 
include using advanced cooling technologies, designing 
energy-efficient architectures, sourcing renewable energy, and 
enhancing 
hardware 
efficiency. 
Policy 
measures 
and 
governance are also crucial to guide the industry toward greener 
practices. Collaborative efforts, investments in research, and 
a focus on renewable energy will help align data centre 
growth with environmental sustainability, ensuring a greener 
digital future. 
Brien Posey et.al. (2022, April 29) [2]:The research focus on heat 
generated in data centres. To mitigate the environmental impact 
of data centres, waste heat recovery technology is considered a 
promising approach. Recovering and utilizing the waste heat 
from data centres for various energy uses, such as heating and 
electricity production, can improve energy efficiency, achieve 
energy and cost savings, and reduce the environmental impact 
caused by both carbon emissions and waste heat discharge. 
Optimizing the heating system, using heat pumps for temperature 
and grade upgrading, and adopting thermal energy storage 
systems can further enhance the efficiency and flexibility of 
waste heat recovery in data centres. 
Charles Liang, et al. (2021, Feb) [3]: Data centres consume 
nearly 3% of the world's power production, with energy 
consumption expected to reach 8% as digital transformation 
increases. Factors like power usage effectiveness (PUE), server 
form factor, refresh cycles, e-waste planning, and use of 
renewable energy can impact a data canter’s. Survey findings 
show IT managers are focused on improving server utilization, 
increasing power density, and advancing cooling technologies to 
make their data centers greener. Strategies to reduce power usage 
and move towards a greener data center, faster refresh cycles, 
server selection, consolidation through virtualization, and 
increasing inlet temperatures. 
Dhanabalan Thangam et al.(2024, March) [4], The number of 
data centres worldwide has surged from 500,000 in 2012 to over 
8 million, with energy consumption doubling every four 
years.The rise in internet penetration rates and the introduction of 
5G technologies and IoT devices will further increase the demand 
for data processing, having environmental impact. The rapid 
growth and increasing reliance on data centers have had a 
significant impact on power consumption, climate change, and 
sustainability. 
Beth Whitehead, Deborah Andrews, Graeme Maidment (2014, 
December) [5]: Data centres are high energy consumers, 
accounting for around a quarter of the ICT industry's emissions. 
The ICT industry as a whole, including data centres, is estimated 
to account for 10% of total UK electricity consumption and 2% of 
global anthropogenic CO2 emissions. The review concludes that a 
more holistic life cycle approach is needed to fully assess the 
environmental impact of data centres. While the industry has 
made efforts to improve operational efficiency, a more 
comprehensive life cycle assessment is needed to fully understand 
and address the broader environmental implications of data centre. 
Ochuko Felix Orikpet, Daniel Ewim (Aug 2023) [6], Data centres 
have a significant impact on climate change due to their growing 
energy demands and greenhouse gas emissions. The paper 
reviews various energy-efficient strategies to mitigate the 
environmental impact of data centres, including: Improving 
energy efficiency through optimized hardware, software, and 
operational practices. Utilizing renewable energy sources to 
power 
data 
centres. 
Implementing 
innovative 
cooling 
technologies to reduce energy consumption. The growing energy 
demands of data centres and their significant contribution to 
greenhouse gas emissions are the key factors that impact the 
environment.  
Hongyu Zhu et al. Feb 2023[7] : The paper mainly studied the 
management of data centers resources, use of clean energy in the 
data centers and building the storage-computing data centers. The 
paper focus on eliminating carbon emission produced by the data 
centers. 
Veerendra 
Mulay 
(5June,2018) 
[8]: 
An important development in data center 
cooling 
technology that can significantlylessen the environmental effect 
of data centers the SPLC systemwhich was created by Facebook  
and Nortek Air Solutions. The SPLC system can cut the water 
usage by over 20% in hot and humid climates and up to 90% in 
cooler climates. This is achieved through the system's ability to 
operate in different modes to optimize water and power 
consumption based on outside temperature and humidity levels. 
This new cooling technology enables Facebook to build highly 
energy and water-efficient data centers in a wider range of 
environmental conditions where direct cooling is not feasible. 
Hence, the SPLC system is used in ssdata centers for cooling that 
can substantially reduce the water and energy consumption of 
these facilities, thereby mitigating their environmental impact. 
Zhi-Ying-Cao ,2023[9]: Data centers can indeed be designed and 
operated to minimize their environmental impact through various 

 
International Journal of Intelligent Systems and Applications in Engineering                          IJISAE, 2024, 12(23s), 3387–3391 |  3389 
sustainable practices. Key factors influencing their sustainability 
include construction materials, energy efficiency technologies, 
and waste management strategies. 
Guo C, et al [10]: This proposed solution is smart grid technology 
that can optimize consumption of energy. This study focuses on 
how to negotiate between the grid suppliers and the data center to 
minimize costs, not necessarily to reduce environmental harms. 
3. Methodology 
 
This research paper employees a mixed-methods approach 
to examine the environmental impacts of data centres, 
focusing on energy consumption, carbon emissions, and 
resource utilization.  
     Quantitative Analysis: 
The quantitative analysis of the environmental impact of 
data centers from 2018 to 2021 highlights critical trends 
across several key areas. From 2018 to 2019, energy 
consumption surged due to increasing power demands, 
leading to higher operational costs and greater cooling 
requirements, which strained local water supplies and 
underscored the need for sustainable management 
practices. The subsequent growth in electronic waste from 
frequent hardware upgrades called for improved recycling 
and disposal strategies, while the rise in the carbon 
footprint emphasized the urgent need for greener 
technologies. This trend continued into 2020 and 2021, 
where rising energy consumption, driven by the demand for 
digital services, further escalated cooling needs and water 
consumption, intensifying the strain on resources. 
Collectively, these trends reflect the pressing challenges 
data centers face and the necessity for sustainable practices 
to mitigate their overall environmental impact. 
 
 
 
Fig 1: Data center energy demand and carbon emission 
 
Data center electricity,global electricity, and GHG emission  is 
represented in blue, red, gray lines in the graph respectively. The 
fig 1 shows the graph that quantifies the energy demands of data 
centers and their contribution to global electricity use and 
greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from 2015 to 2030. Total 
electricity consumption by data centers (TWh) is increasing, total 
global electricity use also grows, but at a slower rate and GHG 
emissions from data centers (in MtCO₂e) are climbing, closely 
tied to electricity demand. 
Qualitative Assessments: 
Existing studies 
will 
be 
reviewed 
to 
identify trends, 
challenges, and innovative practices for reducing data center 
impacts. 
Interviews: Semi-structured interviews with industry experts will 
provide insights into practical challenges and successful 
sustainable practices. 
Surveys: A survey targeting data center managers and IT 
professionals will quantify the adoption of energy efficiency 
measures and renewable energy usage. 
 
4. DATA ANALYSIS: 
The data center industry is only going to continue to grow, the 
best solution is to prioritize a comprehensive strategy that focuses 
on the sustainable construction, design, and maintenance of future 
data centers. Each of these aspects will help reduce the 
environmental implications of data centers.  
We have considered five key environmental impact factors of 
data centers from 2019 to 2024, and provide the mitigation plan  
to reduce the effect on environment. 
a. 
Electricity Consumption (TWh): U.S. data center 
electricity usage has seen a notable increase from 58TWh to 
176 TWh from year 2014 to 2023. Due to AI, IoT, and cloud 
growth, the electricity consumption is projected in 2030 is 
around 800–1,000 TWh globally. In India it is estimated to 
cross 40 TWh/year by 2030.  
Mitigation Plan: 
• Use High-Efficiency Servers & Storage 
• Use of Virtualization & Containerization needed less 
physical servers. 
• Solid-State Drives (SSD) are used rather than Hard 
Disk Drives. 
• Switch to renewable energy. 
b. 
Carbon Emissions (CO₂): This effect heavily on the 
environment. It accelerates climate change, increases 
urban heat islands in tech-heavy cities, acidification of 
oceans due to CO₂ buildup.  
        
Mitigation Plan: 
• 
Use of solar, wind, hydro, and geothermal gives 
zero carbon emmision. 
• 
Having Green PPAs (Power Purchase Agreements) 
contracts. 
• 
Improve energy efficiency by using High-efficiency 
hardware. 
• 
Optimize cooling systems to reduce electricity 
demand and use AI for cooling control. 
c. 
Water Usage (Billion Liters): Data centers use millions of 
liters of water daily for cooling. Global water stress is 
increasing over 50% of the population faces some form of 
water scarcity. India, U.S., and parts of Europe host water-
intensive cloud hubs near already-stressed regions. 
Mitigation Plan: 
• 
Use liquid Cooling, Direct-to-chip or immersion 
cooling reduces total water usage by improving heat 
transfer efficiency. 
• 
Closed-Loop Cooling system recirculates water 
instead of discharging it after one use. 
• 
AI--Driven Cooling Control dynamically adjusts fans, 
pumps, and cooling based on real-time data. 
• 
Predictive Analytics, anticipates heat zones and 
optimizes water use. 
d. 
Cooling Demand (TWh): Higher cooling demand increases 
energy from fossil fuels (unless renewable-powered), 
Carbon footprint, Thermal pollution (when hot water is 

 
International Journal of Intelligent Systems and Applications in Engineering                          IJISAE, 2024, 12(23s), 3387–3391 |  3390 
discharged into local water bodies), Urban heat island effect 
in cities with dense data clusters.  
Mitigation Plan:  
       Use AI-optimized cooling (e.g.,   Google DeepMind), liquid                                                        
or immersion cooling, Free cooling (using outside air), 
thermal containment (hot/cold aisle isolation)    
e. 
E-waste Generation (Million Tons): In 2023, the E-waste 
is approximately 7.5 million tons. The projected E waste in 
2030 is ≥12 million tons globally. 
Mitigation Plan: Hardware Refurbishing is required to 
extends the life of servers. Certified recycling is used to 
reduce the environmental harm. Cloud optimization 
reduces over-provisioning of hardware. 
 
 
Fig 2: Environmental impact of data centers from 2019-2024 
          
 
 
 
Fig 3: Global data center impact in future and India data 
center impact till 2030 
  
Here are two line charts (one in global and second in India) 
showing the projected environmental impact of data centers 
from 2019 to 2030 with respect to above five factors. 
Results:  
The study highlights the significant environmental effects of data 
centers, focusing on important aspects such as trash production, 
water use, energy consumption, carbon emissions, and cooling 
needs. They currently account for 1% to 2% of the world's 
electricity consumption, but by 2030, that percentage might 
increase to 8%, and by 2040, they could account for 14% of 
greenhouse gas emissions. Additionally, data centers use a lot of 
water, which impacts nearby ecosystems, and they produce a lot 
of electronic garbage due to frequent hardware updates, which 
calls for improved recycling procedures. However, hopeful 
remedies are provided by developments in cooling technologies 
and a move toward renewable energy sources.  
The study emphasis the substantial environmental effects of data 
centers, concentrating on crucial elements like waste generation, 
water use, energy consumption, carbon emissions, and cooling 
requirements. Although 1% to 2% share of global electricity 
consumption, by 2030 that number might rise to 8%, and by 
2040, they might be responsible for 14% of greenhouse gas 
emissions. Data centers also generate a lot of electronic waste 
because of frequent hardware upgrades, which necessitate better 
recycling practices, and they require a lot of water, which affects 
the ecosystems in the area. However, advancements in cooling 
technologies and a shift to renewable energy sources provide 
promising solutions. 
Tree plantation is the supportive mechanism to reduce the effect 
on the environment.  Tree absorb carbon dioxide (CO2) from the 
atmosphere through photosynthesis and storing it in their biomass 
(trunks, branches, leaves, roots) and in the soil, called carbon 
sequestration, which plays a vital role in mitigating climate 
change. Trees which have common characterstics like Fast-
growing (absorb more CO2), Long-lived (store carbon longer), 
Large biomass, Dense wood, Large leaves and wide crowns 
(maximum photosynthesis), Native species (support local 
biodiversity) are most effective in carbon sequestration. The trees 
such as Pongamia (Pongamia pinnata), Sal Tree (Shorea robusta), 
Indian Rosewood (Dalbergia latifolia), Mahogany (Swietenia 
macrophylla), Indian Teak (Tectona grandis), Peepal (Ficus 
religiosa), Bamboo (Bambusa balcooa), Matoa (Pometia pinnata) 
can reduce the effect on climate change. 
 
CONCLUSION 
Data centers must adopt sustainable practices to lower their 
environmental impact as they grow. By improving energy 
efficiency, integrating renewable energy sources, and using 
innovative technologies for cooling and waste reduction, the 
industry can curb its carbon footprint and resource use. 
Additionally, better e-waste recycling and sustainable water 
management can protect ecosystems and communities. 
Collaborative efforts are essential, with policymakers, tech 
companies, and environmental organizations all playing key roles 
in setting eco-friendly standards. Through shared commitment to 
responsible resource management and sustainable practices, the 
data center industry can change to support a more sustainable 
digital and environmental future. Addressing these impacts 
requires a multi-faceted approach, including transitioning to 
renewable 
energy, 
implementing 
more 
efficient 
cooling 
technologies, and improving waste management practices. The 
tree plantation is necessary nearby data centers, to reduce 
emissions. Planting the right trees in suitable regions can 
contribute positively 
to 
carbon 
sequestration 
and local 
environmental benefits.
